For some context, `SpecialResource` is used to do cluster hard and soft partitioning. e.g:
- **hard partitioning**: Isolate GPU nodes from the cluster so that only GPU tasks can land on the node.
- **soft partitioning**: any tasks can run on a GPU node until a GPU task is scheduled onto it.

Considering the above operations, `ClusterPartioningPolicy` seems like a possible better fit. What do you think?

@RenaudWasTaken  nouveau was configured by default on the system. Deleting and putting it on the black list fixed the bug!

```
lsmod | grep nouveau
sudo apt-get purge xserver-xorg-video-nouveau-hwe-18.04
sudo bash -c "echo blacklist nouveau > /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-nvidia-nouveau.conf"
sudo bash -c "echo options nouveau modeset=0 >> /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-nvidia-nouveau.conf"
sudo update-initramfs -u
cat /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-nvidia-nouveau.conf
```

Hi @RenaudWasTaken, 
we have multiple GPU and non-GPU nodes in our cluster and one GPU node was reinstalled from scratch and received a more recent kernel version causing the cluster to have GPU nodes with two different kernel versions.

The issue comes now from the restriction that the nvidia driver installation specifies the exact kernel version that it finds on one of the Kubernetes nodes (as in the linked code section above). As the kernel versions differ on this node vs on the other nodes it will not be installed on all GPU nodes but only on the ones with the same kernel version which is specified in the driver installation DaemonSet.
To my understanding this restriction is not needed (also as I understand your comment in https://github.com/NVIDIA/gpu-operator/issues/21#issuecomment-574292501) as the driver is built on each node individually anyways.

In theory it is of course possible to have all nodes on the same kernel version, but at some in time I need to begin updating my nodes e.g. by reinstalling them or removing and adding new nodes to the cluster.
When this starts all new GPU nodes will unusable as the driver installation is not being scheduled there (to my understanding at least from what I see now, I don't know the complete Operator implementation).

Hi @phlp-cg ,

In general I believe the GPU Operator is just meant for mounting the nvidia driver into your containers.

Your container images will still need to have the CUDA runtime/toolkit and the proper environment variables (PATH/LD_LIBRARY_PATH) setup correctly in order to use CUDA applications, just like on a regular machine.

---

I believe one simple/easy way to make sure the image has everything necessary to run CUDA applications is to inherit your image from our NGC CUDA images in your Dockerfile. 

For example,
```
# Dockerfile
FROM nvcr.io/nvidia/cuda:10.0-devel-ubuntu18.04

# Install dependencies
# ...

# Install cupy
# ...
```

Please note that I believe only the CUDA images with the tag `*-devel-*` will come with everything you need pre-configured for running CUDA apps.

At the current state it seems not that simple to customize operator's deployments.
In my case :
* nvidia-container-toolkit-daemonset is deployed from a static asset file https://github.com/NVIDIA/gpu-operator/blob/master/assets/state-container-toolkit/0400_container_toolkit.yml
* This file is parsed by the operator, format is auto-detected from object Kind and then added to the resources managed by the controller (in a clusterPolicyController object).
* This object is modified by preprocess functions (preProcessDaemonSet) that overrides image and tag from ENV vars (inside getToolkit func)
* This ENV var is loaded from a ConfigMap in some Helm templates (operator-configmap.yaml). It holds only the processed image path of the toolkit docker image.

This is a bit unusual (and complex) behavior for k8s operators.
So in the current state of this project, I think the best way would be to add an additional ENV var with a custom yaml and then deep merge this yaml in the specs inside the existing preProcessDaemonSet function ...

But it's rather rewrite everything and directly manipulate kube objects in code instead of seeing static assets in repo blindly parsed like this :'(

@relyt0925 I have installed and run the nvidia GPU operator on OpenShift 4.3. I focus mainly on clusters that are not connected to the internet. There are a few quirks to how the operator/helm chart are setup which require tuning in an air-gapped environment.

I have not tried to use the web console to deploy the operator and I'm not sure exactly what error you're running into but by default this operator won't work without some setup.

OpenShift 4 AWS IPI deploys all nodes as RHCOS. Nvidia built their driver images for RHCOS based on UBI images from RedHat. Nvidia all built the driver image such that it determines the kernel version of the RHCOS host at run time, dnf installs packages, and builds the nvidia kernel model. That dnf part can be a problem. Because the Nvidia gpu operator images are based on UBI images they do not have access to the standard RHEL repo stream. RHCOS also doesn't include these streams. To deploy on OpenShift you have to do one of 2 things:

- Add RHEL entitlements into your OpenShift cluster that has all RHCOS nodes so the nvidia UBI driver image can dnf install packages
- Add a RHEL node to your cluster, with a GPU, so that the driver is deployed on that host. The UBI image will inherit the entitlements from the underlying RHEL node.

If you are supporting disconnected environments I can send you some details on how to do that. I have a repo where I tossed what I did to build the driver image for disconnected environments. TL;DR you have to know the kernel version of the host the image will run on.

**Third finding**: There is no doc to what an example spec for the CR should look like, and if you just apply the given template it fails looking for exporter spec. I found this and it worked for me:

`
apiVersion: nvidia.com/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: cluster-policy
spec:
  dcgmExporter:
    image: dcgm-exporter
    repository: nvidia
    version: 1.7.2-2.0.0-rc.11-ubi8
  devicePlugin:
    image: k8s-device-plugin
    repository: nvidia
    version: 1.0.0-beta6-ubi8
  driver:
    image: driver
    repository: nvidia
    version: 440.64.00
  operator:
    defaultRuntime: crio
  toolkit:
    image: container-toolkit
    repository: nvidia
    version: 1.0.2-ubi8
  size: 4
`

Issue Solved:
     The issue with the failed drivers for nVidia appear to be a "repository" issue with RedHat.  

If you are not properly subscribed, when you run the following command, you will see the output below.
```
oc logs nvidia-driver-daemonset-5pn8w -n gpu-operator-resources, 

dnf install -q -y elfutils-libelf.x86_64 elfutils-libelf-devel.x86_64
Error: Unable to find a match: elfutils-libelf-devel.x86_64
```
To address the issue with the subscriptions:
1.  Ensure you are properly subscribed via the RedHat site
2.  Use this link and do steps 1 and 2 on your cluster or you can follow the entire Helm portion:  https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/kubernetes/openshift-on-gpu-install-guide/index.html#openshift-gpu-install-gpu-operator-via-helmv3
##The above section appears to be left out of the process for using the Operators.  It's either a documentation issue or it's a development issue that the Operators are not doing "yet".

If you are properly subscribed, and you see the following error, this is a versioning issue.  The nVidia driver that is attempting to install requires the kernel-headers and the kernel-devel packages.  This in turn links back to the subscription.  The issue come into play with the channel repositories that RedHat has available.  For version 4.3.28, the RedHat coreOS kernel is 4.18.0-147.20.1.el8_1.x86_64.  This package is not published/available with the subscription.  In order to facilitate the installation, we had to upgrade to version 4.3.33 which updates all the workers to version 4.18.0-193.14.3.el8_2.x86_64.  When you run the #oc logs cluster-entitled-build-pod -n default, you should see that kernel version listed in the entitlements.
```
+ dnf -q -y install kernel-headers-4.18.0-147.20.1.el8_1.x86_64 kernel-devel-4.18.0-147.20.1.el8_1.x86_64
Error: Unable to find a match: kernel-headers-4.18.0-147.20.1.el8_1.x86_64 kernel-devel-4.18.0-147.20.1.el8_1.x86_64
```

Summary:
1.  Ensure you have your cluster properly entitled
2.  Check versions to ensure support

@aheifetz I was able to get the GPU driver working in a 4.5.9 cluster this week using a nvidia driver container image that I created myself. Nvidia based their GPU operator on Red Hat's UBI images but installs RPMs that are not part of the UBI repos. It uses RPMs that are part of core RHEL. This is why a RHEL sub is required to build the driver images for the GPU operator when used on OpenShift 4. The easiest way around this is to just build the driver independently on an internet connected RHEL server and then update the helm chart to use your own images. I do this in ansible with helm like:

```
        /usr/local/bin/helm install \
            nvidia-gpu-operator \
            --namespace default \
            --set 'platform.openshift=true,operator.defaultRuntime=crio' \
            --set "driver.repository={{ mirror_registry }}:{{ mirror_registry_port }}/nvidia"
            --set "driver.version=450.51.06-1.0.0-custom-rhcos-4.18.0-193.13.2.el8_2.x86_64-4.5.2"
            --set "toolkit.repository={{ mirror_registry }}:{{ mirror_registry_port }}/nvidia"
            --set "devicePlugin.repository={{ mirror_registry }}:{{ mirror_registry_port }}/nvidia"
            --set "dcgmExporter.repository={{ mirror_registry }}:{{ mirror_registry_port }}/nvidia"
            '{{ mirror_base }}/helm/gpu-operator-1.1.7.tgz'
```

Note that while the image tag above ends in 4.5.2 the helm chart will append rhcos-4.5 so when you push the image to your internal registry you'll need to account for that.

I digged into this a bit again as I saw the same issue in 1.1.7 (just try the command from above) and it seems that it appears due to the confusing helm behaviour when specifying the `--namespace` parameter, especially to `helm template`, see e.g. https://github.com/helm/helm/issues/3553#issuecomment-521424132 .
`--namespace` is only effective when `{{ .Release.Namespace }}` is used AND when applying to the k8s cluster - it doesn't set `namespace: ...` on every object as you might expect for `helm template`.

Also before https://github.com/NVIDIA/gpu-operator/commit/8501fd7929234855b60975e7c9902f536c82d920 the namespace parameter was specified in some locations making this a bit more confusing. It seems now that the `helm` way is to have an extra tool patching the namespace on every source as it is an `computationally expensive ordeal` (quote) for helm.

The operator runs a daemonset called `container-toolkit` with the container from this project installed:
https://gitlab.com/nvidia/container-toolkit/container-config

When launching this container, the operator sets up the following mount from the host into the container:
```
      volumes:
        - name: docker-socket
          hostPath:
            path: /var/run/docker.sock
        - name: nvidia-install-path
          hostPath:
            path: /run/nvidia
        - name: docker-config
          hostPath:
            path: /etc/docker
        - name: nvidia-local
          hostPath:
            path: /usr/local/nvidia
        - name: crio-hooks
          hostPath:
            path: /etc/containers/oci/hooks.d
```

The container itself, has the full `nvidia-docker` stack with all of its bins and libs installed inside of it at standard locations (i.e. `/usr/local/bin` and `/lib64`).

At startup, the `container-tooolkit` daemonset will run the following script:
https://gitlab.com/nvidia/container-toolkit/container-config/-/blob/master/src/run.sh

This script does the following:
1) Gather all of the components of the nvidia-docker stack and copy them under `/usr/local/nvidia/toolkit`
2) Update the contents of `/etc/docker/daemon.json` to configure the default container runtime to `/usr/local/nvidia/toolkit/nvidia-container-runtime`
3) Restart the docker daemon

Since `/usr/local/nvidia/`, `/etc/docker/`, and `/var/run/docker.sock` are all mounted from the host into the container, all of these changes are reflected on the host, and not just inside the container (even the docker restart).

With standalone containerd, a similar "patching" of `/etc/containerd/config.toml` could be done, but it is not yet supported by the operator. We plan to add support for this in the next release (`v1.4.0`).

We also plan to make the locations of the files mounted on the host configurable (at present it is assumed that the host path is the same as the container path for all mounts) so that non-root instances of docker / containerd can be supported (as is necessary for things like `microk8s`, which run their own instance of `containerd` from a `snap` sandbox).

> I believe this is because of a race condition between the driver container and the device plugin.


I think the issue comes from the usage of `DaemonSet` for deploying the GPU operator:

```
NAME                                 DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   NODE SELECTOR                 AGE
gpu-feature-discovery                1         1         1       1            1           nvidia.com/gpu.present=true   15h
nvidia-container-toolkit-daemonset   1         1         1       1            1           nvidia.com/gpu.present=true   15h
nvidia-dcgm-exporter                 1         1         1       1            1           nvidia.com/gpu.present=true   15h
nvidia-device-plugin-daemonset       1         1         1       1            1           nvidia.com/gpu.present=true   15h
nvidia-driver-daemonset              1         1         1       1            1           nvidia.com/gpu.present=true   15h
```

when rebooting or adding a new node with `nvidia.com/gpu.present=true`, the DaemonSets will *all* (re)create Pods on the nodes, all at the same time, without any control of the GPU operator.

Eventually the Pod of the `nvidia-driver-daemonset` will load the `nvidia` driver. But _as far as I've seen_, the `nvidia-device-plugin-daemonset` Pod cannot detect the GPU when it restarts. It needs to be manually destroyed (and automatically recreated) to detect it.

1. Installing Docker-CE and `nvidia-docker2` as described in the documentation
1. Using the GPU Operator in a Kubernetes environment

When you're using the GPU Operator you don't need to install the NVIDIA driver, `nvidia-docker2` etc. You only need to ensure that Docker is available on the system. 
When you're just running GPU containers on the system (outside of K8s with the GPU Operator), then you need to install the NVIDIA drivers, `nvidia-docker2` and Docker on the system.

`containerd` support is coming in the 1.4.0 release of the GPU operator (scheduled for release this week).

Here is a list of the PRs that enabled it:
https://gitlab.com/nvidia/container-toolkit/container-config/-/merge_requests/40
https://gitlab.com/nvidia/container-toolkit/container-config/-/merge_requests/43
https://gitlab.com/nvidia/kubernetes/gpu-operator/-/merge_requests/145

The following flags can be used to control `containerd` support in `values.yaml`:
```
operator:
  defaultRuntime: containerd

toolkit:
  env:
  - name: CONTAINERD_CONFIG
    value: /etc/containerd/config.toml
  - name: CONTAINERD_SOCKET
    value: /run/containerd/containerd.sock
  - name: CONTAINERD_RUNTIME_CLASS
    value: nvidia-container-runtime
  - name: CONTAINERD_SET_AS_DEFAULT
    value: true
```

First you set the `runtime` to `containerd` under the `operator` component. Then then you customize the specific `containerd` settings via environment variables on the `toolkit` component.

The settings I’m showing above for the `toolkit` component are the default ones if you don’t set them to anything at all.

In the context of `microk8s`, you would want to set `CONTAINERD_CONFIG` and `CONTAINERD_SOCKET` to point to the `containerd` config and socket files inside the `snap` sandbox.

The `CONTAINERD_RUNTIME_CLASS` variable can then be optionally set to customize the name of the `runtime-class` associated with the `nvidia-container-runtime` in the `containerd` config file.

Likewise, `CONTAINERD_SET_AS_DEFAULT` can be optionally set to toggle whether you want the `nvidia-container-runtime` to be the *default*  runtime used by `containerd` (i.e. when launching containers in a pod without an explicit `RuntimeClass`), or whether you only want it to only be used when a pod sets its `RuntimeClass` to match the name set in `CONTAINERD_RUNTIME_CLASS`.

@kitch Could you please explain it in detail? Is this a bug with CentOS?

No. It is an issue with the underlying NVIDIA container stack.

It executes a binary called `nvidia-container-cli` which has a dependence on a shared library called `libnvidia-container1.so`. This library, in turn, has a shared library dependence on `libc.so`. 

The issue comes from the fact that `nvidia-container-cli` and `libnvidia-container1.so` are pulled out of the `container-toolkit:1.3.0` image and copied onto the host as part of the toolkit installation process. When `nvidia-container-cli` is executed on the host it then links to the `libnvidia-container1.so` library that was copied along with it from the `container-toolkit:1.3.0` image, but links to the _host_ `libc.so` library (which on `centos` is a different version of `libc.so` than the one contained in the `container-toolkit:1.3.0` image which is based on ubuntu). This then causes the error you are seeing.

The reason that switching to the `container-toolkit:1.3.0-ubi8` fixes the issue, is because the `nvidia-container-cli` and `libnvidia-container1.so` libraries are dependent on the `libc.so` version present in the `container-toolkit:1.3.0-ubi8` image -- which is now the same version of `libc.so` present on the `centos` host.

There are two was to fix this:
1. Bundle `libc.so` with the `nvidia-container-cli` and `libnvidia-container1.so` copied over from the container
2. Statically link `nvidia-container-cli` so that it no longer has these shared-library dependencies

The plan forward is to go with (2)

> The following table shows the helm settings available for configuring the GPU operator with containerd support.
> ```
> operator:
>   defaultRuntime: containerd
> 
> toolkit:
>   env:
>   - name: CONTAINERD_CONFIG
>     value: /etc/containerd/config.toml
>   - name: CONTAINERD_SOCKET
>     value: /run/containerd/containerd.sock
>   - name: CONTAINERD_RUNTIME_CLASS
>     value: nvidia
>   - name: CONTAINERD_SET_AS_DEFAULT
>     value: true
> ```
> The only required setting is for `operator.defaultRuntime` to be set to `containerd`. This will trigger the GPU operator to load the “Container Toolkit” with `containerd` support. The rest of the settings are optional and are used to customize specific `containerd` settings under the hood. The values shown here are the defaults.
> 
> `CONTAINERD_CONFIG`: The path on the host to the `containerd` config you would like to have updated with support for the `nvidia-container-runtime`. By default this will point to `/etc/containerd/config.toml` (the default location for `containerd`). It should be customized if your `containerd` installation is not in the default location.
> 
> `CONTAINERD_SOCKET`: The path on the host to the socket file used to communicate with `containerd`. The operator will use this to send a `SIGHUP` signal to the `containerd` daemon to reload its config. By default this will point to `/run/containerd/containerd.sock` (the default location for `containerd`). It should be customized if your `containerd` installation is not in the default location.
> 
> `CONTAINERD_RUNTIME_CLASS`: The name of the [Runtime Class ](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/containers/runtime-class/)you would like to associate with the `nvidia-container-runtime`. Pods launched with a `runtimeClassName` equal to `CONTAINERD_RUNTIME_CLASS` will always run with the `nvidia-container-runtime`. The default `CONTAINERD_RUNTIME_CLASS` is `nvidia`.
> 
> `CONTAINERD_SET_AS_DEFAULT`: A flag indicating whether you want to set `nvidia-container-runtime` as the default runtime used to launch all containers. When set to false, only containers in pods with a `runtimeClassName` equal to `CONTAINERD_RUNTIME_CLASS` will be run with the `nvidia-container-runtime`. The default value is `true`.
> 
> Below is an example of launching the GPU Operator with `containerd` support with explicit values for each of the optional settings described above.
> ```
> helm install --wait --generate-name \
>     nvidia/gpu-operator \
>     --set operator.defaultRuntime=containerd \
>     --set toolkit.env[0].name=CONTAINERD_CONFIG \
>     --set toolkit.env[0].value=/etc/containerd/config.toml \
>     --set toolkit.env[1].name=CONTAINERD_SOCKET \
>     --set toolkit.env[1].value=/run/containerd/containerd.sock \
>     --set toolkit.env[2].name=CONTAINERD_RUNTIME_CLASS \
>     --set toolkit.env[2].value=nvidia \
>     --set toolkit.env[3].name=CONTAINERD_SET_AS_DEFAULT \
>     --set toolkit.env[3].value=true

Since the gpu-operator is failing when there are no gpu-nodes (see details), **we don't see the periodic scale up that @ranjb describes.**

We're running cronjobs this way:
* A cronjob that requires gpu is triggered
* Clusterautoscaler provisions a gpu-instance
* The Job runs to completion
* Clusterautoscaler terminates the gpu-instance

This is **very cost efficient** and should therefore be supported.

### Details

When there is no gpu instance:
```
NAME                                                              READY   STATUS      RESTARTS   AGE
gpu-operator-657579678c-sfjl8                                     0/1     Error       13         13h
```
Output:
```
{"level":"info","ts":1609319235.8210428,"logger":"controller_clusterpolicy","msg":"Could not get any nodes to match nvidia.com/gpu.present label","Request.Namespace":"default","Request.Name":"Node","ERROR":""}
{"level":"info","ts":1609319235.8210719,"logger":"controller_clusterpolicy","msg":"Failed to apply transformation 'nvidia-driver-daemonset' with error: 'ERROR: Could not find kernel full version: ('', '')'"}
```

### Workaround:
**Warning: this is hacky and no large scale approach**
Schedule a "warmup" job that requires gpu 15 minutes before the *actual* cronjob to trigger the gpu-instance creation ahead of time.
This allows the cluster to stabilize and get everything in order, before the job is run.
The drawback here, is that it'll cost you 15 minutes of compute and you'll have the gpu-operator in an error-state whenever a job is not running (annoying to have failing pods around, I know).

Example:
```
> kubectl get cronjob

NAME                            SCHEDULE     SUSPEND   ACTIVE   LAST SCHEDULE   AGE
train-model-gpu-job-warmup      0 9 * * *    False     1        4m2s            37d
train-model-gpu-job           	15 9 * * *   False     0        19m             27d
```




You may need to experiment with the delay in your own cluster.

Hi again. I found the problem. The A100 had mig enabled. This was a leftover of a previous experiment where i enabled MIG with `nvidia-smi -mig 1`. I was not aware that this setting is stored in the GPU itself and survives a host reinstall.

After i reverted the GPUs mig setting, the validation pod worked fine. I'm really sorry, that i wasted your time :(

I'm left with the question though how mig and the operator could work together at this stage. I'm aware that 1.4.0 is currently not ready for mig (as mentioned by @klueska in https://github.com/NVIDIA/gpu-operator/issues/128) and expects manual intervention. I can open a dedicated issue to handle this question if you like.

I think I may have gotten to the bottom of this issue.

When `libnvidia-container` starts up, one of the first things does is load the `nvidia` kernel module (if not already loaded) as well as create the `/dev/nvidiactl`, `/dev/nvidia-uvm`, `/dev/nvidia-modeset`, and `/dev/nvidia*` device nodes on the host file system (so that it can simply mount them in later as necessary).

https://github.com/NVIDIA/libnvidia-container/blob/master/src/nvc.c#L192..L218

Later on it selectively bind-mounts these devices into the container as necessary (depending on which devices should be injected as well as what capabilities are set):

https://github.com/NVIDIA/libnvidia-container/blob/master/src/nvc_mount.c#L616..L619

When adding MIG support, I added the code to bind-mount any necessary `nvidia-capabilities` from `/dev/nvidia-caps` into a container to give it access to a MIG device (or enable it to configure / monitor a set of MIG devices depending on the capability):

https://github.com/NVIDIA/libnvidia-container/blob/master/src/nvc_mount.c#L655..L658

However, I didn't add the logic to pre-create these device nodes on the host at startup time. Which means that if they donÄt already exist -- the `libnvidia-container` will fail to bind-mount them and throw an error.

So regarding....

> A workaround to propagate the MIG slicing is to call nvidia-smi -L inside the driver-daemonset local Pod. This will have the side effect to propagate the MIG reconfiguration and make it visible to all the existing and new Pods

By running `nvidia-smi` in the driver container, you are triggering the creation of these device nodes on the host, so they are available the next time `libnvidia-container` attempts to bind-mount them.

This obviously answers why this would fix things for new pods, but it is still a mystery to me why it would suddenly make them visible to existing pods (unless they have the driver's `/dev` folder (i.e. `/run/nvidia/driver/dev`  mounted in over their `/dev` folder).

In any case, I will look into adding the proper fix into `libnvidia-container` to pre-create these nodes before the bind mount.

Thanks again for reporting this important issue.

It's not supported at this time. Building Driver Container from Docker by hand would be the easiest to hack together. You would need to edit the distro-specific script (e.g. `ubuntu20.04/nvidia-driver`) to apply the arguments and paths for the public and private keys, and bind mount the public and private keys.
A more production-ready solution would need access to public/private keys whenever GPU operator starts the Driver Container, because it can at any time trigger a driver build. I don't like the idea of letting an automated system hold onto driver signing keys. I would prefer from a security stand point not to implement this and have it remain a manual process initiated by a cluster administrator.

The operator supports both `v1` and `v2` configs for `containerd`.  The `v1` config is only technically required for `containerd` 1.2, while either `v1` or `v2` should be usable by `containerd` 1.3+.

As some background, the `default_runtime_name` parameter is not technically part of the `v1` config spec, and (if set) definitely causes issues when using the operator with `containerd` version 1.2. Interestingly, however, it seems to be OK when used in a `v1` config with `containerd` 1.3+, even though it#s not technically part of the `v1` spec.

For the `v1` spec, you are supposed to use the `default_runtime` section to specify what the default runtime should be, which is what we do here: https://github.com/NVIDIA/container-config/blob/master/src/containerd.go#L320

For the `v2` spec, the `default_runtime_name` parameter you mention, was introduced to avoid the need for a separate `default_runtime` section (which for `v1` often times just ended up duplicating some other `runtime` section). We set the `default_runtime_name` for `v2` configs here: https://github.com/NVIDIA/container-config/blob/master/src/containerd.go#L481

In your particular situation, you seem to be running a version of `containerd` which supports the `v1` spec, but somehow *requires* the setting of `default_runtime_name` in the `v1` spec (which technically shouldn't be necessary or allowed).

In your PR you seem to add support for `default_runtime_name` to our handling of the `v1` spec (which can't be done, because it will break support for `containerd` 1.2), and you duplicate the logic we already have for `default_runtime_name` in the `v2` spec (making the change unnecessary).

In general, the reason you are seeing the `v1` spec at all (even though you are on a newer version of `containerd` which supports the `v2` spec ) is because we fallback to writing a config from the `v1` spec in situations where no previous config existed. In theory, all supported versions of `containerd` (i.e. 1.2, 1.3, and 1.4) should be able to parse and apply a `v1` config even if they also support `v2`.  It seems that your version doesn't do this as expected though.

As such, I think the right fix is to add logic in the toolkit container to actually inspect the `containerd` version and explicitly only apply the `v1` config for `containerd` 1.2, and the `v2` config for 1.3 and 1.4 (unless of course a `v1` config is already in place which I expect to be rare).

ah - sorry 🤦 . I should have suggested proper steps. Please install `nvidia-fabricmanager-<driver-branch>` package from the CUDA repos (not the `cuda-drivers-fabricmanager` since that is a meta package that ensures the driver and FM are installed together). The `nvidia-fabricmanager` package has no other dependencies so is a better choice. Once that is installed, you can do `systemctl --now enable nvidia-fabricmanager` to start the `systemd` service. Then proceed to install the GPU operator.

I found the recipe. I'm using microk8s on Ubuntu 20.04, here's what I had to do to make this work on both a Nvidia DGX A100 as well as a ProLiant DL380 Gen10 machine with T4 GPU.

- Make sure to start on a fresh Ubuntu 20.04 with no nvidia drivers (or `apt purge` the nvidia packages if you can't)
- blacklist the nouveau driver (add `modprobe.blacklist=nouveau nouveau.modeset=0` to `GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT` in `/etc/default/grub` and run `sudo update-grub` and reboot)
- [for the A100 only] Install the package `nvidia-fabricmanager-460` from the cuda repos (you won't be able to enable the systemd service until the K8s GPU operator has loaded the drivers)
- Install microk8s with the 1.21/beta channel (I have version v1.21.0-beta.1)
- `microk8s enable dns` (tip: make sure your DNS is working by launching a test pod and resolving internal and external hostnames)
- `microk8s enable gpu`
- [for the A100 only] enable nvidia-fabricmanager (`sudo systemctl --now enable nvidia-fabricmanager`)

@chuempel this is more a VMware ESXi issue. Recent CPUs from Intel and AMD implement a machine-check architecture that detects and reports hardware issues, including system bus errors, RAM (ECC and parity) errors, and other CPU errors. There are a set of model-specific registers (MSRs) that are used to report errors. When a hardware error occurs, global and bank-specific status machine-check architecture registers are populated with information regarding the cause, and whether the CPU can safely continue execution. In the case of a correctable error, ESXi reports the incident and register contents in the VMkernel logs. If an error is uncorrectable, and the CPU cannot continue safely, ESXi halts with a purple diagnostic screen.

Read the crash log from ESXi by following this procedure: https://kb.vmware.com/s/article/1006796

The operator installs all of the driver software on the host under `/run/nvidia/driver`. As such, it will be made available to containers launched on Kubernetes (via the nvidia-container-toolkit), but is not (immediately) available to programs running on the host.

If you are trying to run `nvidia-smi` from the host (which it appears you are), then the easiest way to do this is to run it while `chroot`ed into `/run/nvidia/driver`, i.e.
```
chroot /run/nvidia/driver nvidia-smi
```

@xhejtman This is one of the limitation we have with driver container currently. Driver container goes through these steps each time:

1. Unload any existing modules
2. Unmount root filesystem of driver installation on host (**/run/nvidia/driver)**
3. Fetch prerequisites for driver compilation
4. Compile and package drivers
5. Install new driver package along with other CUDA libraries and utilities.
6. Load updated driver modules
7. Bind mount driver root filesystem / onto host at **/run/nvidia/driver**

Once the modules are already loaded, as long as something is holding a reference to it, we cannot unload it. Also, when driver container exits, driver root filesystem on host is inaccessible as well. Only way to restore from this point is to perform host reboot. We are looking to re-architect driver container, but it might be a while.

Do you know the reason why driver container was restarted?

@amrmahdi The main reason for not adding any `update` logic within gpu-operator is due to `driver` container. We cannot let driver container restart  on the fly as it will cause the bind mounted driver install path on host (/run/nvidia/driver) to become stale and would require a node reboot. Another reason is Helm itself doesn't support upgrade of CRD's. Due to this restriction, we always recommended to un-install and re-install GPU operator for any updates.  Having said that, we are working on a solution to let driver upgrades work in a rolling fashion and also to handle upgrade of other components(dcgm, gfd, device-plugin etc). But Helm limitations with CRD's will likely not go away anytime soon, so user would still need to manually update ClusterPolicy CRD prior to operator upgrade.

@d-m Since the ClusterPolicy spec handles creation of eight Daemonsets, size of the CR has become huge. Yes, the limitation with `last-applied-configuration` annotation will break upgrades. Since all Daemonset values needs to be configurable, not sure we can overcome this with single CRD we have. eg driver spec is below:

```
driver:
  enabled: true
  repository: nvcr.io/nvidia
  image: driver
  version: "460.73.01"
  imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
  imagePullSecrets: []
  env: []
  tolerations:
  - key: nvidia.com/gpu
    operator: Exists
    effect: NoSchedule
  nodeSelector:
    nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.driver: "true"
  affinity: {}
  podSecurityContext: {}
  securityContext:
    privileged: true
    seLinuxOptions:
      level: "s0"
  resources: {}
  # private mirror repository configuration
  repoConfig:
    configMapName: ""
    destinationDir: ""
  # vGPU licensing configuration
  licensingConfig:
    configMapName: ""
  priorityClassName: system-node-critical
```

With the limitation on max size of CR(which will end up in `last-applied-configuration` annotation), it would make sense to split each Daemonset config into a separate CRD (i.e NvidiaDriver, NvidiaDevicePlugin, NvidiaDCGMExporter, NvidiaGPUFeatureDiscovery, NvidiaMIGManager, NvidiaContainerToolkit, NvidiaValidator) and individual CR's control configuration for each Daemonset we deploy.

Currently we don't support upgrade of ClusterPolicy types, so un-install and install is always recommended. We are looking to support upgrades in future releases, so this will be a design discussion we will have.

Please refer [here](https://github.com/NVIDIA/gpu-operator/blob/master/bundle/1.7.1/manifests/gpu-operator.clusterserviceversion.yaml#L142) and add this along with `nodeSelector` fields for all components. We are removing the nodeSelector as configurable from next version, but with 1.7.1 it should be explicitly specified in ClusterPolicy instance.
Hi @shivamerla. 1.6.x applied nodeSelectors (nvidia.com/gpu.present: 'true') automatically to all DaemonSets. Did this change in 1.7.x?

@geoberle yes, now each component has a nodeSelector label as below. GPU operator will automatically add these labels to nodes with NVIDIA GPU's. The reason for this granularity is to evict individual component pods when required(for eg MIG config change requires device-plugin, GFD pods to be evicted on the node and started again).

```
                    nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.mig-manager=true
                    nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.container-toolkit=true
                    nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.dcgm-exporter=true
                    nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.device-plugin=true
                    nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.driver=true
                    nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.gpu-feature-discovery=true
                    nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.operator-validator=true
```

As we don't expect user to change these values, it should have been added by default, but was missed in `1.7.x`. So these have to be specified in ClusterPolicy instance as defined [here](https://github.com/NVIDIA/gpu-operator/blob/master/bundle/1.7.1/manifests/gpu-operator.clusterserviceversion.yaml#L142).

@koflerm Unloading an existing driver is little involved when driver container restarts. We are automating this with next upcoming release. Meanwhile you will need to evict all other GPU operator pods on each node at a time with below command.

```
    oc label --overwrite \
        node ${NODE_NAME} \
        nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.operator-validator=false \
        nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.container-toolkit=false \
        nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.device-plugin=false \
        nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.gpu-feature-discovery=false \
        nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.dcgm-exporter=false
```

Once all are evicted, driver pod can be restarted to let it cleanly `rmmod` existing driver and install again.  Once driver is loaded, you can re-run all these pods again by setting the labels to `true`. Same has to be repeated on each node.

Hi everyone,

This issue is not a bug with the nvidia driver-container. The driver-container requires that the kernel-headers for the running kernel are present and can be accessed by the package manager (i.e. yum, dnf) inside of the driver-container. The issue is, if you are running a kernel that is slightly out of date, meaning it is the not the latest kernel version, the package manager will probably not be able to access the right kernel-headers by default and therefore the driver-container will fail like above.

To avoid this issue, either 1) Upgrade your running kernel, or 2) Provide a custom repo configuration file for the driver container by configuring the `driver.repoConfig` option when deploying the gpu-operator. This solution isn't documented yet, but we will be documenting these steps soon on our official [docs](https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/cloud-native/gpu-operator/overview.html).

@sakaia Looks like you are installing with runtime set to `containerd`, but toolkit is disabled. So you need to manually configure `/etc/containerd/config.toml` in this case. You seem to have configured /etc/docker/daemon.json instead. Below is an example of how containerd config should looks like.

```
$ cat /etc/containerd/config.toml 
version = 2

[plugins]

  [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri"]
    sandbox_image = "k8s.gcr.io/pause:3.4.1"

    [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd]
      default_runtime_name = "nvidia"

      [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes]

        [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.nvidia]
          privileged_without_host_devices = false
          runtime_engine = ""
          runtime_root = ""
          runtime_type = "io.containerd.runc.v1"

          [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.nvidia.options]

The WITH_REBOOT env variable is set here in `values.yaml`. Its an environment variable for the migManager pod.
https://github.com/NVIDIA/gpu-operator/blob/832f3175889625005e711c7c49d314e100d52892/deployments/gpu-operator/values.yaml#L215

To set the value of this variable, you can either directly download and modify `values.yaml` prior to running `helm install -f values.yaml gpu-operator`. The -f flag will use your modified `values.yaml` file instead of our default.

Or you can set that variable via the command line (not sure if there is a better/more concise way of doing this with --set):

`helm install gpu-operator --set migManager.env[0].name=WITH_REBOOT --set migManager.env[0].value=true`

So for anyone interested, I managed to solve my issue. It was in fact caused by a selinux 'bug' on the host running the container. Apparently a new lockdown class was introduced for selinux in Fedora 34 and this was an unwanted side-effect (https://www.spinics.net/lists/fedora-devel/msg284833.html). I just created a selinux policy on the host running the container to go around the problem and now I can insert kernel modules from the container.

In general, the `k8s-mig-manager` does not automate the process of ensuring that it is "OK" to change the MIG configuration on the GPUs that it manages. It assumes that some higher level entity is coordinating the setting of the `mig.config` label on the node when it is OK to do so.

At present, best practice before applying a MIG config change to any GPU is to:
1. Cordone the node
2. Wait for all GPU jobs to complete
3. Apply the `mig.config` label to change the MIG config
4. Wait for the MIG config change to complete
5. Uncordone the node

We didn't want to be prescriptive and automate all of these steps in the `k8s-mig-manager` itself because SRE teams typically already have their own process for doing 1, 2 and 5, and now they can just integrate the setting of the `mig.config` label into that process when desired.

The toolkit validator does not (and should not) rely on `chroot`ing into the root of the driver installation, because the whole point of this validator is to verify that the `toolkit` is working (which means that all GPU related software will be injected into the container automatically by the toolkit instead of requiring a chroot into the driver's root fileystem).

Can you show the contents of your `/etc/containerd/config.toml` after the toolkit has been deployed? It should have been modified to set up a new `nvidia` runtime that will be used to start the validator (and actually all) subsequent containers.

**Note:** Your `ctr` test will always fail with the `toolkit` validator because we don't configure the `runtime.v1.linux` plugin for containerd to work with the `nvidia-container-runtime`.  We only configure the `cri` plugin, which is needed for kubernetes.

### Environment:
OS: Ubuntu 20.04.3 LTS (5.4.0-91-generic)
Kubernetes: K3s v1.22.3+k3s1
Containerd: 1.5.7-k3s2

### Steps taken

#### 1. Verify NVIDIA device

After a lot of frustration, I discovered the GPU wasn't listed in `lspci`. I would suggest as a first step to make sure the node shows your NVIDIA card by running `lspci | grep NVIDIA`. 

> NOTE: In my particular case, using a Lenovo P340 Tiny, I had to have the VGA Mode set to `Auto` in the BIOS.

#### 2. Disable Nouveau

Disable Nouveau on the GPU node. Follow the docs [here](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-installation-guide-linux/index.html#runfile-nouveau-ubuntu).

> NOTE: I didn't see this called out in the Operator docs any more so this may no longer be needed

#### 3. Install Drivers

I could not get the install driver functionality of the Helm Chart/Operator to work. I suspect it only supports the Enterprise/Datacenter GPUs. I imagine this could be customized to install the appropriate drivers for my GPU but for me it was easier to simply install the drivers manually. To do this, run:

```bash
apt-get update && \
apt-get install nvidia-headless-470-server nvidia-utils-470-server
```

> NOTE: 470 was the latest as of this writing. Check for the latest by running `apt-get search nvidia-driver`

#### 4. Install Operator

Install the Operator via the Helm Chart. You can mostly follow the directions [here](https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/cloud-native/gpu-operator/getting-started.html#install-the-gpu-operator) but use the following Helm values:
```yaml
dcgm:
  enabled: false
migManager:
  enabled: false
driver:
  enabled: false
toolkit:
  enabled: true
  env:
    - name: CONTAINERD_CONFIG
      value: /var/lib/rancher/k3s/agent/etc/containerd/config.toml
    - name: CONTAINERD_SOCKET
      value: /run/k3s/containerd/containerd.sock
    - name: CONTAINERD_RUNTIME_CLASS
      value: nvidia
    - name: CONTAINERD_SET_AS_DEFAULT
      value: "true"
```

For me, I needed to disable the Datacenter features of `dcgm` and `migManager` as I am not using a DC GPU. You need to override the default containerd values as k3s installs these in a non-default location. By doing this, I noticed my `/var/lib/rancher/k3s/agent/etc/containerd/config.toml` was updated with:

```toml
[plugins.cri.containerd.runtimes."nvidia"]
  runtime_type = "io.containerd.runc.v2"
[plugins.cri.containerd.runtimes."nvidia".options]
  BinaryName = "/usr/local/nvidia/toolkit/nvidia-container-runtime"

[plugins.cri.containerd.runtimes."nvidia-experimental"]
  runtime_type = "io.containerd.runc.v2"
[plugins.cri.containerd.runtimes."nvidia-experimental".options]
  BinaryName = "/usr/local/nvidia/toolkit/nvidia-container-runtime-experimental"
```

This is a bit different than what the [Docs](https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/cloud-native/gpu-operator/getting-started.html#bare-metal-passthrough-with-pre-installed-drivers-and-nvidia-container-toolkit) say and is what got me hung-up.

Converts the current centos image into rocky

```
FROM nvcr.io/nvidia/driver:470.82.01-centos8

# Edit yum configs to use vault repos
RUN sed -ri 's|^mirrorlist|#mirrorlist|' /etc/yum.repos.d/*.repo \
    && sed -ri 's|^#baseurl|baseurl|' /etc/yum.repos.d/*.repo \
    && sed -ri 's|^metalink|#metalink|' /etc/yum.repos.d/*.repo \
    && sed -ri 's|mirror.centos.org|vault.centos.org|g' /etc/yum.repos.d/*.repo

# Convert from CentOS to RockyLinux
RUN yum -y install \
        ncurses \
    && curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rocky-linux/rocky-tools/main/migrate2rocky/migrate2rocky.sh -o migrate2rocky.sh \
    && chmod +x migrate2rocky.sh \
    && sed -ri '/^efi_check$/d' migrate2rocky.sh \
    && ./migrate2rocky.sh -r \
    && rm migrate2rocky.sh \
    && yum -y remove \
        ncurses \
    && yum clean all

# Add older kernels
RUN set -x; \
    ROCKYLINUX_VERSIONS=($(curl -sL https://dl.rockylinux.org/vault/rocky | egrep -o "8.[0-9]+" | sort -u)); \
    for v in ${ROCKYLINUX_VERSIONS[@]}; do \
        yum-config-manager --add-repo=http://dl.rockylinux.org/vault/rocky/${v}/BaseOS/x86_64/os; \
    done

# Upgrade gcc
RUN yum -y upgrade \
        gcc \
    && yum clean all
```

CATALOG_PORT=$(echo "${CATALOG_SERVICE}" | yq -r ".spec.ports[0].targetPort")

echo "Querying the catalog ..." >&2

LIST_BUNDLES=$(oc run $QUERY_PODNAME  \

                  --restart=Never \
                  --attach=true \
                  --image=$GRPCURL_IMAGE \

            )
ret=$?

if [ ! $ret == 0 ]; then
    echo "ERROR: failed to fetch the list of bundles">&2
    exit 1
fi

echo "Bundles for $PACKAGE_NAME:" >&2
echo "$LIST_BUNDLES" | jq -c 'select(.packageName=="'$PACKAGE_NAME'")|{packageName,channelName,csvName}'

@chrisholzheimer 
> apt seem to only raise a warning, but it seems nvidia-driver-daemonset pod still need packages from official repos to work:

Yes, these packages are required for the driver container to work.

> If we rebuild image including our local repositorys the driver pod is working:

Instead of rebuilding the image, you can follow [these instructions](https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/cloud-native/gpu-operator/appendix.html#local-package-repository) for mounting a custom repo config file into the driver daemonset so that your local repository mirror is used.

> get a list of all GPUs installed in a cluster and their additional info.

Most of the components in the gpu-operator are daemonsets - so they would report devices found on a per node basis. If you're using something like Prometheus then you would have to aggregate that info across all the nodes in your cluster. For example, the node description (e.g. using `kubectl describe node`) would use the info from the device plugin to determine how many GPUs have been enumerated and available for allocation. 

Are you looking for a singular query that lists out the GPUs across your entire cluster? That wouldn't exist at the NVIDIA software component level without aggregation. 

> UUIDs

Yes - they uniquely identify every GPU that has ever been/will be shipped.

One other thing to check if `nvidia` runtime is set to default or not in `/etc/containerd/config.toml`, if not then you need to specify `runtimeClass` attribute in podSpec to use `nvidia` runtimeClass.

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: cuda-vectoradd
spec:
  restartPolicy: OnFailure
  runtimeClassName: nvidia
  containers:
  - name: cuda-vectoradd
    image: "nvidia/samples:vectoradd-cuda11.6.0"
    resources:
      limits:
         nvidia.com/gpu: 1
```

@shivamerla I can see in the other issue that this is causing a lot of confusion. Therefore, I propose:

a: default the ImagePullPolicy to Always, as the driver images receive bugfixes without increasing the version
=> this will automatically fix this problem, but might cause problems in the future when a previously working driver image gets corrupted for some reason

b (preferred): update the chart/operator to pin the image. I.e., use the image digest (sha) to select the correct image.
=> This will give the users more fine control, is more deterministic, and eases debugging.

Either way, IMHO the chart should be updated to `1.10.2` which contains either (a) or preferably (b) to fix this issue and possibly upcoming issues.

During further investigation, this issue was found to be related to the behavior difference when switching from precompiled to compiled drivers during the upgrade.

In gpu-operator v25.3.x, driver.usePrecompiled was enabled .
In gpu-operator v25.10.0, it was changed to false (precompiled drivers disabled), which switches the setup from precompiled to compiled drivers.

This change modified the driver DaemonSet by removing the nodeSelector added for precompiled drivers. As a result, Kubernetes detected a DaemonSet change and triggered an automatic rollout of the driver pods. This rollout bypassed the OnDelete strategy, and the upgrade controller did not get a chance to manage GPU workload eviction on multi-node clusters. When GPU workloads were still running, this led to the Init:CrashLoopBackOff issue.

To validate this behavior, the following test was performed:

- Installed gpu-operator v25.3.x with driver.usePrecompiled=true
- Patched ClusterPolicy to disable precompiled drivers before upgrade
- Ensured all pods were stable
- Upgraded to gpu-operator v25.10.0

In this scenario, there was no change in the driver DaemonSet during the upgrade, no automatic rollout was triggered, the upgrade controller executed correctly, GPU workloads were terminated, and the issue did not occur.

This confirms that the DaemonSet change caused by switching from precompiled to compiled drivers is a key trigger for this problem.

Hi @moditanisha22, thank you for the detailed report. This looks like a feature we don't support as of today.

We currently support following driver installations:
1. Compiled drivers managed by clusterpolicy
2. Precompiled drivers managed by clusterpolicy
3. Compiled drivers managed by nvidiadriver
4. Precompiled drivers managed by nvidiadriver

We don't support seamless upgrades from one type to another as of today. In your case, upgrade or switch was done from precompiled to compiled drivers.

In case of precompiled driver with clusterpolicy, the driver daemonset name would be something like:
```
k get daemonset -n gpu-operator | grep driver
nvidia-driver-daemonset-5.15.0-171-generic-ubuntu22.04   1         1         1       1            1           feature.node.kubernetes.io/kernel-version.full=5.15.0-171-generic,nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.driver=true   3d20h
```
In case of compiled driver with clusterpolicy, the driver daemonset name would be something like:
```
k get daemonset -n gpu-operator | grep driver
nvidia-driver-daemonset                      1         1         1       1            1           nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.driver=true                                      2d19h
```
Since you changed from pre-compiled to compiled, entire daemonset would be deleted and new daemonset created, and there is no seamless migration of driver pods from one daemonset to another. If this switch (from one type to another) is done before upgrading to newer release/driver version, then only driver daemonset's content will change during upgrade and upgrade-controller will take care of rolling out all driver pods in a controlled manner.

I am marking this issue as an enhancement we can look to support in future.

Integrates the [NVIDIA DRA Driver for GPUs](https://github.com/NVIDIA/k8s-dra-driver-gpu) as a first-class managed operand within the GPU Operator. DRA (Dynamic Resource Allocation) is a Kubernetes-native mechanism (GA in k8s 1.32) for fine-grained, structured device sharing — an alternative to the classic device plugin model. The GPU Operator can now deploy and lifecycle-manage the DRA driver alongside existing operands.

### 1. New API Surface (`ClusterPolicy`)
Adds a `draDriver` section to `ClusterPolicySpec` with two sub-features:
- `draDriver.computeDomains` — enables the compute-domain DRA driver (IMEX/NVLink fabric topology, multi-node GPU cliques)
- `draDriver.gpus` — enables the GPU DRA driver (structured GPU resource advertising via `ResourceSlice`); **mutually exclusive** with the device plugin
### 2. New State: `state-dra-driver`
New manifests under `assets/state-dra-driver/`:
- ServiceAccounts for driver and compute-domain daemon
- ClusterRoles/Roles/Bindings for controller, kubelet-plugin, compute-domain daemon
- 4 DeviceClass objects: `compute-domain-daemon`, `compute-domain-default-channel`, `gpu`, `mig`
- Controller Deployment
- ConfigMap for driver config
- DaemonSet for DRA kubelet-plugin (privileged on OpenShift via dedicated RoleBinding)
### 3. Controller Integration
- `state_manager.go` — new `StateDRADriver` handler registered in the state machine
- `object_controls.go` — ~290 lines of DRA reconciliation (controller Deployment, kubelet-plugin DaemonSet, ConfigMap); applies standard GPU Operator transforms (image overrides, tolerations, resource limits)
- `resource_manager.go` — updated for DRA cluster-level permissions
### 4. Validation (Two Layers)
- **Helm-time** (`validation.yaml`): blocks install/upgrade if DRA enabled on non-DRA cluster, or device-plugin + DRA GPUs both enabled
- **Operator-time** (`clusterpolicy_validator.go`): checks `resource.k8s.io` API group at startup; sets `ClusterPolicy` notReady with human-readable error if DRA requested but not supported
### 5. Helm Chart Updates
- `values.yaml`: new `draDriver.computeDomains.*` and `draDriver.gpus.*` values (disabled by default)
- `clusterrole.yaml` / `role.yaml` expanded with DRA permissions
- `clusterpolicy.yaml` template updated
- CRDs regenerated; `upgrade_crd.yaml` / `cleanup_crd.yaml` updated for ComputeDomain CRD
### 6. Tests
- Unit tests in `controllers/transforms_test.go` (+330 lines) for DRA object transforms
- Manual E2E documented in PR: non-DRA cluster (error path), DRA cluster with compute-domains only, DRA cluster with GPU DRA (device-plugin disabled)

| Decision | Rationale |
|---|---|
| DRA GPUs mutually exclusive with device-plugin | Prevents double-allocation of the same GPU resources |
| ComputeDomains can coexist with device-plugin | Compute-domain (IMEX) resources are distinct from raw GPU resources |
| Disabled by default | DRA requires k8s ≥1.32; safe opt-in for existing users |
| DeviceClass apiVersion conditional | Handles both `v1alpha3` (k8s 1.31) and `v1beta1` (k8s 1.32+) |
| OpenShift privileged via separate RoleBinding | Follows existing GPU Operator pattern for OpenShift SCCs |

Hi @FermiX9, thanks for the detailed report. I took a look at what's happening under the hood, here's a breakdown of the issue and some things you can try.

When MIG is enabled on B200 GPUs and containerd is running, all GPU operator pods are scheduled simultaneously on the node, each pod needs to interact with the NVIDIA kernel driver during initialization, either via `nvidia-smi` or NVML library calls.

With MIG profile `1g.23gb`, each physical GPU is partitioned into ~8 instances, meaning the driver must enumerate significantly more device handles. When containerd is running, the `nvidia-container-runtime` plugin also holds NVML handles to these devices, creating lock contention at the kernel driver level, which explains the 5s - 44s slowdown you observed.

The problem is that multiple pods hitting the driver concurrently during startup creates a "query storm" that pushes response times past the configured timeouts.

AFAIU the timeout comes from:

1. **Driver container startup probe**, The startup probe script runs `nvidia-smi` directly:
   - Script: [`assets/state-driver/0400_configmap.yaml` (line 24)](https://github.com/NVIDIA/gpu-operator/blob/main/assets/state-driver/0400_configmap.yaml#L24)
     ```sh
     if ! nvidia-smi; then
       echo "nvidia-smi failed"
       exit 1
     fi
     ```
   - Probe config: [`assets/state-driver/0500_daemonset.yaml` (lines 140-149)](https://github.com/NVIDIA/gpu-operator/blob/main/assets/state-driver/0500_daemonset.yaml#L140-L149) , `timeoutSeconds: 60`, `periodSeconds: 10`, `failureThreshold: 120`
   - Defaults defined in: [`internal/state/driver.go` (lines 533-546)](https://github.com/NVIDIA/gpu-operator/blob/main/internal/state/driver.go#L533-L546)

   With `nvidia-smi` taking 44s+ under contention (and likely longer with multiple concurrent callers), the 60s timeout is barely sufficient, and under a pod startup storm, it's exceeded.

2. **Downstream pod init containers** , GFD, device-plugin, DCGM exporter, and MIG manager all have an init container that polls for a validation file:
   - [`assets/gpu-feature-discovery/0500_daemonset.yaml` (lines 29-32)](https://github.com/NVIDIA/gpu-operator/blob/main/assets/gpu-feature-discovery/0500_daemonset.yaml#L29-L32)
   - [`assets/state-device-plugin/0500_daemonset.yaml` (lines 29-31)](https://github.com/NVIDIA/gpu-operator/blob/main/assets/state-device-plugin/0500_daemonset.yaml#L29-L31)
     ```yaml
     args: ["until [ -f /run/nvidia/validations/toolkit-ready ]; do echo waiting for nvidia container stack to be setup; sleep 5; done"]
     ```
   These block indefinitely until the toolkit validation file is created, which itself depends on the driver being ready.

3. **Operator validator**, runs sequential init containers (`driver-validation` - `toolkit-validation` - `cuda-validation` - `plugin-validation`) in [`assets/state-operator-validation/0500_daemonset.yaml`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/gpu-operator/blob/main/assets/state-operator-validation/0500_daemonset.yaml). The plugin validation step uses a hard-coded GPU resource discovery timeout of **150 seconds** (30 retries × 5s) defined in [`cmd/nvidia-validator/main.go` (lines 194-197)](https://github.com/NVIDIA/gpu-operator/blob/main/cmd/nvidia-validator/main.go#L194-L197):
   ```go
   gpuResourceDiscoveryWaitRetries     = 30
   gpuResourceDiscoveryIntervalSeconds = 5


If the device-plugin hasn't registered MIG resources within 2.5 minutes (because it's also stuck waiting for slow NVML calls), this validation fails.

4. **GFD/device-plugin NVML calls**,  since you have the driver installed on the host (not managed by the operator), these components call NVML directly during their own initialization. NVML hits the same kernel driver locks as nvidia-smi, so they experience the same contention and slowness.

I believe s possible workaround would be to:

1. Increase the startup probe timeout via `ClusterPolicy`. The ClusterPolicy CRD exposes probe configuration on the DriverSpec ([api/nvidia/v1/clusterpolicy_types.go lines 528-535](https://github.com/NVIDIA/gpu-operator/blob/main/api/nvidia/v1/clusterpolicy_types.go#L528-L535))

```
apiVersion: nvidia.com/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
spec:
  driver:
    startupProbe:
      initialDelaySeconds: 120
      timeoutSeconds: 120
      periodSeconds: 15
      failureThreshold: 180
```

Since you have the driver on the host, this won't directly apply — but if you're using the NVIDIADriver CRD, the same fields are available in [api/nvidia/v1alpha1/nvidiadriver_types.go](https://github.com/NVIDIA/gpu-operator/blob/main/api/nvidia/v1alpha1/nvidiadriver_types.go).

2. If you can temporarily set nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.gpu-feature-discovery: "false" and nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.device-plugin: "false" as node labels, you can let the toolkit/driver validation complete first, then enable the other components one at a time by flipping labels back to "true". This avoids the concurrent NVML query storm.

I believe the root cause is that the operator doesn't account for the kernel driver lock contention that occurs on GPUs with many MIG instances + an active container runtime. A propere fix would require to deploy all daemonsets simultaneously and relying on init container polling, the operator could enforce an ordering where each component fully initializes before the next one starts on a given node and perhaps make the hard-coded `gpuResourceDiscoveryWaitRetries = 30` and `gpuResourceDiscoveryIntervalSeconds = 5` in [cmd/nvidia-validator/main.go](https://github.com/NVIDIA/gpu-operator/blob/main/cmd/nvidia-validator/main.go#L194-L197) exposed as configurable parameters (e.g., via environment variables), so operators can increase the 2.5-minute window for environments where NVML calls are slow

Existing behavior/code kind of works for us because role, rolebinding, clusterrole, clusterrolebinding, configmap, serviceaccount, service, deployment, daemonset allow updates without resource version (unconditional update = true).

Ex:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/537ab630b23903686992b4cfb905ff7a412becbf/pkg/registry/rbac/role/strategy.go#L97-L104
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/537ab630b23903686992b4cfb905ff7a412becbf/pkg/registry/apps/deployment/strategy.go#L148-L150

I am not sure what is the better approach here. Current change does adds additional Get() call to get revisionVersion and avoid concurrent updates (uses cache though). But we don't have concurrent updates for these resources as of today (maybe we will once we enable/support HA?). Also, with the new change, we are going GET before doing CREATE or UPDATE and that will help in avoiding all the CREATE calls we were making till today on every reconcile as the resource would be there and we would be just updating it after that.

Also, we can also use patch instead of update to reduce the amount of data sent to apiserver.

I would like to get others thoughts on tradeoffs and improvement and if we should get this change in.
Perhaps we could consider using https://pkg.go.dev/sigs.k8s.io/controller-runtime/pkg/controller/controllerutil#CreateOrUpdate?

I was going to suggest this. If we don't strictly need `update`, can we just use `patch`? We had changed some update calls to patch for K8s node updates in our controller logic before. So far, they have worked fine and have also solved problems of node update race conditions when we encountered them in the past.

Hi @framsouza ,

Thank you for the detailed explanation.
After increasing the workload in our Kubernetes cluster, we've observed that this behavior is not limited to the GPU Operator pods. It also affects regular GPU workloads.

The issue is reproducible after rebooting a node:
When all Deployments that request GPU resources, or otherwise need to query the NVIDIA driver, start at roughly the same time, several pods get stuck during startup and eventually fail with `context deadline exceeded`.

However, if we first scale GPU-related workloads down to 0 and then bring them back gradually, pods start successfully.

Because of that, we believe this may not be strictly a GPU Operator issue, but rather a driver/MIG issue that becomes visible under concurrent startup pressure.

Hi @futurewasfree, 

As mentioned in https://github.com/NVIDIA/k8s-driver-manager/issues/138, we've merged [k8s-driver-manager#166](https://github.com/NVIDIA/k8s-driver-manager/pull/166) to improve the logging here, but we did not change the underlying behavior because it is working by design.

The GPU Operator has two mutually-exclusive ways to handle workload eviction during a driver upgrade:

1. **Upgrade controller** (when `driver.upgradePolicy.autoUpgrade: true`) owns drain/eviction at the controller level.
2. **k8s-driver-manager** (when `autoUpgrade: false`) honors `ENABLE_GPU_POD_EVICTION` / `ENABLE_AUTO_DRAIN` env vars from the init container.

When `driver.upgradePolicy.autoUpgrade=true` in the `ClusterPolicy` CR, GPU driver upgrades are facilitated by the gpu-operator's driver-upgrade controller (see the [state machine](https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/cloud-native/gpu-operator/latest/gpu-driver-upgrades.html#upgrade-state-machine)). The controller is the entity that evicts GPU clients and optionally drains the node. We purposely disable the GPU pod eviction and node drain logic in the `k8s-driver-manager` init container because those operations should only be performed by the controller. We rely on the upgrade-controller to handle GPU workload eviction in a controlled manner when explicitly required, and we avoid forcibly evicting GPU workloads during `k8s-driver-manager` restarts. Many training jobs are long-running (spanning hours or even days), and premature eviction could result in loss of progress or critical inference data. The `ENABLE_GPU_POD_EVICTION` / `ENABLE_AUTO_DRAIN` env vars are intentionally superseded in this mode; they apply only when `autoUpgrade: false`.

If your driver pod is stuck unloading the kernel module, the holder is often a pod that doesn't declare `nvidia.com/gpu` in its resource requests. Neither the upgrade controller nor `k8s-driver-manager` can reliably detect those and it's a known limitation. If you hit this, the new log message from [#166](https://github.com/NVIDIA/k8s-driver-manager/pull/166) spells out four recovery options.

I will be closing this issue but feel free to follow up with any questions or concerns.

Thanks for the report. This is working as designed, but the current log message buries that — we've merged [k8s-driver-manager#166](https://github.com/NVIDIA/k8s-driver-manager/pull/166) to replace `disabled by the upgrade policy` with explicit recovery guidance.                                                                                          
                                                                                                                             
When `driver.upgradePolicy.autoUpgrade=true` in the ClusterPolicy CR, GPU driver upgrades are facilitated by the gpu-operator's driver-upgrade controller (see the [state machine](https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/cloud-native/gpu-operator/latest/gpu-driver-upgrades.html#upgrade-state-machine)). The controller is the entity that evicts GPU clients and      optionally drains the node. We purposely disable the GPU pod eviction and node drain logic in the `k8s-driver-manager` init container because those operations should only be performed by the controller — `ENABLE_GPU_POD_EVICTION` / `ENABLE_AUTO_DRAIN` apply only when `autoUpgrade: false`. We avoid forcibly evicting GPU workloads during `k8s-driver-manager` restarts since many training jobs are long-running (hours or days), and premature eviction could result in loss of progress or critical inference data.

For your specific repro: switching `driver.usePrecompiled` between `true` and `false` during an upgrade changes the driver DaemonSet's name, so the old DaemonSet is deleted and a new one is created. The upgrade controller never gets a turn to move the node through its state machine, which is why you saw the driver pod restart immediately without workload eviction. Cross-type migrations (precompiled ↔ compiled) are not currently supported as a seamless upgrade path — flip `usePrecompiled` first on the existing version, let the cluster settle, then perform the version upgrade.

If you hit the stuck-driver-pod state again, the new log message from #166 spells out four recovery options.

Closing this out — please reopen if the new message still doesn't unblock you.

Environment
Platform: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) v1.35.x
GPU Operator chart version: v25.3.x (deployed via Flux HelmRelease)
Monitoring stack: Azure Managed Prometheus (ama-metrics addon)
Problem
The gpu-operator chart hard-codes monitoring.coreos.com/v1 as the API group for its ServiceMonitor CRD. This is baked into the Go source (resource_manager.go imports promv1 "github.com/prometheus-operator/prometheus-operator/pkg/apis/monitoring/v1") and there is no chart value to override the API group.

On AKS with Azure Managed Prometheus, the ama-metrics agent only scrapes CRDs registered under azmonitoring.coreos.com/v1. ServiceMonitors using monitoring.coreos.com/v1 are ignored entirely — metrics are never collected.

Impact
GPU metrics (DCGM Exporter) are unavailable in Azure Managed Grafana/Prometheus when using the gpu-operator's built-in serviceMonitor.enabled: true
Users must manually create a separate azmonitoring.coreos.com/v1 ServiceMonitor outside the chart as a workaround
This affects all AKS clusters using Azure Managed Prometheus (the default monitoring path for AKS)
Requested Change
Add a configurable value (e.g., serviceMonitor.apiGroup or serviceMonitor.apiVersion) that allows overriding the ServiceMonitor API group from the default monitoring.coreos.com to an alternative like azmonitoring.coreos.com.

Example:
dcgmExporter:  
     serviceMonitor:    
     enabled: true    
     apiGroup: "azmonitoring.coreos.com"  # NEW — defaults to "monitoring.coreos.com"

Workaround
Currently we deploy a separate ServiceMonitor manifest targeting azmonitoring.coreos.com/v1 outside the chart, duplicating configuration that the chart should could natively.

Thanks for the report! This is expected behavior.

The `gpu-operator` controller listens for node label events, so when labels disappear and reappear it triggers reconcile events that cause the operator to reset the `nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.*` labels.  Modifying these label values isn't a recommended production practice — it's intended as a convenience for users who need to quickly undeploy an operand for testing. 

In this case, a plausible workaround is to set the label back after NFD rewrites them. 

Closing as this a known limitation, but please feel free raise any follow up questions or concerns.

**Manual reproduction on OpenShift 4.21.5 / GCP — confirmed the bug**

**Environment:**
- OpenShift 4.21.5 on GCP (`us-central1`)
- GPU Operator `v26.3.1` (certified-operators)
- NFD `4.21.0-202604200440` (redhat-operators)
- Node: `n1-standard-4` with 1x NVIDIA Tesla T4

**Steps to reproduce:**

1. Installed GPU Operator with `devicePlugin.enabled: true` — all pods healthy, metric baseline:
   ```
   gpu_operator_node_device_plugin_devices_total{node="...gpu-worker-a-zdd2q"} 1
   ```

2. Patched ClusterPolicy to `devicePlugin.enabled: false`:
   ```
   oc patch clusterpolicy gpu-cluster-policy --type merge -p '{"spec":{"devicePlugin":{"enabled":false}}}'
   ```

3. Device plugin pod terminated as expected. After kubelet refresh, GPU capacity cleared:
   ```
   nvidia.com/gpu capacity: 0
   nvidia.com/gpu allocatable: 0
   ```

4. Metric dropped to `0`:
   ```
   gpu_operator_node_device_plugin_devices_total{node="...gpu-worker-a-zdd2q"} 0
   ```

5. Queried Prometheus — `GPUOperatorNodeDeploymentFailed` alert entered **pending** state immediately:
   ```json
   {
     "name": "GPUOperatorNodeDeploymentFailed",
     "state": "pending",
     "alerts": [{
       "state": "pending",
       "activeAt": "2026-05-01T15:21:33.613957041Z",
       "value": "0e+00"
     }]
   }
   ```
   This will fire after the 30m `for:` duration — a false positive.

**Confirmed root cause:** The node-status-exporter has no awareness of the `devicePlugin.enabled` setting. Its env vars are only `NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, COMPONENT, METRICS_PORT, NODE_NAME, OPERATOR_NAMESPACE` — no `DEVICE_PLUGIN_ENABLED`. The alert expression `gpu_operator_node_device_plugin_devices_total == 0` cannot distinguish "intentionally disabled" from "failed deployment."

Hi @rjhaikal! This issue is two-fold.

The `popd` error comes from the container's entrypoint script — I believe it is not fatal and mostly cosmetic but worth fixing. I'll make a note of it. 

The GSP firmware failure is what actually crashes the pod. My best guess is that this is a deployment/build issue. I know this issue is from over a year ago,  but one thing worth checking is whether your pod logs contain the line `A search path is already configured in /sys/module/firmware_class/parameters/path`. The vGPU manager entrypoint has an explicit branch that declines to overwrite that sysfs value if it's already set, and silently keeps whatever was there. If that warning is present, the host's firmware search path is pointing somewhere other than `/run/nvidia/driver/lib/firmware`


Please let me know if this is an issue that you're still facing. 

EDIT: closing the issue now as it's quite stale and an initial solution was provided. Please feel free to re-open to open a new issue if this persists.

On v25.3.1 with correctly-running CTK, `toolkit-validation` still execs `nvidia-smi` ~40s before CTK finishes writing the nvidia containerd config, and the pod CrashLoopBackOffs.

Root cause: [`WITH_WAIT=false`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/gpu-operator/blob/v25.3.1/assets/state-operator-validation/0500_daemonset.yaml#L87-L88) on `toolkit-validation`, while `driver-validation` and `nvidia-fs-validation` use `WITH_WAIT=true` against already-written markers. Happy to PR the default flip, unless there's a design reason for the asymmetry.

@anoopsinghnegi Thanks for the detailed report! This looks to be an edge case when nodes reboot during repartitioning. Could you clarify a few things so any possible fix lands in the right component?

1. When `mig.config.state=pending` and the label disappears, what's the state of the driver pod? Does `nvidia-smi` return any devices?
2. Is the `gpu-feature-discovery` pod on that node running, paused (`nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.gpu-feature-discovery=paused-for-mig-change`), or crash-looping? GFD logs around the time the label was removed would help.
3. Could you share the full set of node labels and the `NodeFeature` CR for the affected node when it's in the stuck state?

Context for why I'm asking: the `nvidia.com/gpu.product` label is owned by GFD (in `k8s-device-plugin`), and the `-INVALID` suffix you referenced is add only when MIG mode is enabled but slices aren't configured, not when devices can't be enumerated. If GFD is seeing zero devices, it returns no labels and NFD garbage-collects the existing ones, which matches what you're seeing. This is a bit tricky since GFD would have to persist last-known state across restart, which it's not designed to do currently.

Thanks for the question.

NVIDIA does publish prebuilt vGPU guest driver containers on NGC for supported Ubuntu and RHEL/RHCOS environments, but those images are part of NVIDIA AI Enterprise and are only accessible to entitled NVAIE customers. They are not public GPU Operator driver images.

For NVAIE customers, the documented path is to use the NVAIE GPU Operator installation flow with an NGC API key / image pull secret so the cluster can pull the restricted vGPU guest driver image from NGC:
https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/cloud-native/gpu-operator/latest/install-gpu-operator-nvaie.html

For users who are not NVAIE-entitled, or who specifically want to use the Azure GRID driver packages distributed by Microsoft, there is not a public NVIDIA-provided Azure GRID driver container image. In that case, the available options are:

1. Use the AKS-managed/preinstalled NVIDIA driver path and install GPU Operator with driver management disabled.
2. Build and host a private driver container using driver bits you are entitled to use, then configure `NVIDIADriver` / GPU Operator to pull from that private registry.
3. For Azure-specific GRID packaging or licensing questions, follow up with Microsoft/Azure support, since those installers are distributed through Microsoft’s Azure documentation.

So the short answer is: yes, NVIDIA has vGPU guest driver containers on NGC, but access is restricted to NVAIE customers; they are not generally available public images for all AKS/Azure GRID users.

1. How many nodes were there in the cluster?
2. Were all driver pods immediately terminated and new driver pods created?

Was there a specific reason you were going from precompiled drivers to dynamic driver compilation during upgrade? We don't support controlled driver migration from precompiled to compiled via upgrade controller. If you are switching between them, all driver pods will be terminated immediately and new driver pods will be created on the entire cluster. They don't go through upgrade controller and hence you would be seeing driver pods in crashloop state waiting for GPUs to be released before driver can be updated. Any node which still has active pods using GPUs will see driver pod stuck as it needs no workload to be using the GPU before it can unload and reload the kernel module.

By labeling the node as "upgrade-required", you are forcing upgrade-controller to kick in and manage upgrade of the driver on that node. Upgrade controller would then be evicting pods using GPUs so that driver installation can proceed further.

Once driver installation has succeeded and all other operands have restarted after that and come up fine, upgrade controller will then label the node as upgrade-done to indicate it is in stable state. Since you were transitioning from precompiled -> compiled and that doesn't go through controlled migration/upgrade using upgrade controller, you might see nodes still labeled as upgrade-done even though driver or other operands on those nodes are still in transitioning state. Upgrade controller kicks in the very end just to label the node as upgrade-done if all operands are running fine on that node.

I am still not clear about the intermediate "upgrade-failed" seen by you which then fixes by itself to "upgrade-done". I would recommend trying out driver upgrade while keeping only one approach (precompiled or dynamic drivers). We can then see whats going on in that setup. Also, 25.3.0 is quite old now, I would recommend trying latest versions to see if you still see the issue there.
