You're right about the operator's own dcgm-exporter - the driver-manager evicts it during an in-place upgrade. Ours is a standalone dcgm-exporter deployed outside the operator, so the driver-manager doesn't know about it and doesn't evict it. But I'll be upfront that dcgm-exporter is the weaker example, and we do intend to move to the operator's bundled exporter once a site is fully on the operator (more on the "why standalone" below).

The primary consumers this PR is for are our inference workloads, not dcgm-exporter:

 - Triton and the NVIDIA VST (vms) pods run with runtimeClassName: nvidia and no nvidia.com/gpu resource request. We run them in exclusive mode (no time-slicing / MPS) so each gets native performance and full VRAM on small edge GPUs (e.g. an 8 GB Quadro RTX 4000), with several consumers sharing the device through the runtime rather than the device plugin.
 - Because they don't request nvidia.com/gpu, the targeted GPU-pod eviction (which keys on that resource via the PodDeletionFilter) never selects them. In our in-place upgrade testing on an edge node, these pods kept the driver module pinned and the upgrade stalled at pod-restart-required until we deleted them by hand. Freeing them let the operator unload, rebuild and reload the driver in place with no reboot.

So the gap is GPU consumers that use the device via the nvidia runtime without a resource request: they're invisible to the upgrade eviction. The PodSelector lets us declare them so the operator frees them itself, without forcing them onto a resource-request / time-slicing model we deliberately avoid on these GPUs.

On why the standalone dcgm-exporter: we run GPU metrics across a fleet of 400+ edge servers, most of which are still on bare-metal NVIDIA drivers rather than the operator. The standalone exporter gives us one metrics pipeline that behaves the same against bare-metal and operator-managed drivers. Moving to the operator's bundled dcgmExporter has to be a paired, per-site change (enable the operator's exporter and remove the standalone, since the two can't co-exist on a node), which we can't roll out fleet-wide while most sites are still bare-metal. It's transitional - we expect to retire it per site as sites finish migrating. The durable justification for this PR is the runtime-direct inference workloads above.

This overlaps with a sibling need on the vGPU / sandbox path, and I think the two are worth solving with one mechanism.

This issue asks for `FABRIC_MODE=1` (Shared NVSwitch) plus a reachable FM command socket for the DRA driver's passthrough / VFIO path. The SR-IOV **vGPU** path (`nvidia.com/gpu.workload.config=vm-vgpu`) needs the same two things, but with `FABRIC_MODE=2` (vGPU multitenancy): in mode 0 a vGPU guest reports fabric status "Insufficient Permissions"; only in mode 2 can a per-VM fabric partition be activated, which is what lets a whole-card (NVLink-enabled) vGPU guest initialize CUDA — otherwise `cuInit` returns 802 ("system not yet initialized").

Today the operator manages no FM mode on the vGPU path at all:

- the bare-metal driver daemonset starts `nv-fabricmanager` from the driver-container entrypoint, always in the default bare-metal mode (`FABRIC_MODE=0`), with no operator knob to change it — `FABRIC_MODE` appears nowhere in `gpu-operator` or `gpu-driver-container`;
- the vGPU host-manager container's entrypoint does not start or manage Fabric Manager at all;
- with a host-installed driver, the operator manages nothing FM-related.

So enabling vGPU on an NVSwitch node currently requires installing FM and setting `FABRIC_MODE=2` out-of-band on each host.

Proposal: make the FM fabric mode configurable (0 / 1 / 2) and expose the FM command/SDK socket at a shared, host-reachable location for **both** the passthrough (mode 1) and vGPU (mode 2) paths, rather than solving mode 1 alone. The per-VM partition activation itself is out of scope for the operator — for vGPU the consumer activates the single-GPU partition per VF at allocation time (see NVIDIA/kubevirt-gpu-device-plugin#193, which Addresses NVIDIA/kubevirt-gpu-device-plugin#133). The operator only needs to provide FM running in the correct mode with a reachable socket.

Happy to help scope the vGPU side if that's useful.

Hi @ctrlsam, thank you for the context; it's certainly helpful. 

We are working on some changes that will help users get third-party (to gpu-operator) gpu clients to be restarted during a driver upgrade. If testing goes well, they will make it into the next planned release of the gpu-operator (`v26.7.0`). This is primarily for adding the capability to bounce third-party daemonsets that require admin access to the GPUs (bypassing the k8s-device-plugin).

That said, I would still discourage uses like this the one you've mentioned below:

>  We run them in exclusive mode (no time-slicing / MPS) so each gets native performance and full VRAM on small edge GPUs (e.g. an 8 GB Quadro RTX 4000), with several consumers sharing the device through the runtime rather than the device plugin.

Have you looked into time-slicing instead? With time-slicing, the available GPU numbers are artificially inflated by the device plugin and this way your workloads should get access to all the GPUs so that you get the desired performance. The advantage here is that your workload pods will get evicted automatically by the gpu-operator as the workload pods would end up getting selected by the gpuPodDeletion filters as noted by you earlier. More details on time slicing can be found [here](https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/cloud-native/gpu-operator/latest/gpu-sharing.html).

It's good to hear the third-party client eviction is landing in v26.7.0.

On time-slicing, my hesitation comes from this benchmark comparing the sharing modes on a saturated GPU: https://github.com/nebuly-ai/nos/tree/main/demos/gpu-sharing-comparison. Time-slicing average inference time scales close to linearly with the number of co-located pods (roughly 0.09s at 1 pod -> 0.29s at 3 -> 0.49s at 5 -> 0.69s at 7), where MPS stays much flatter and MIG is flat. For real-time inference that linear latency growth under contention is the thing I'm wary of.

That said, the benchmark is about 3 years old now (driver 525, k8s 1.24), so my real question is whether it's still representative. @tariq1890 has there been changes to time-slicing scheduling or the driver since then that would materially change that curve, or is linear degradation under saturation still the expected behaviour?

I don't want to argue from a stale benchmark either way. I'll start running our own over the next week on our actual edge hardware and workload (p50/p99 inference latency, current runtime-direct sharing vs time-slicing, at our real consumer counts) and share the numbers here. If time-slicing holds up against our latency targets it's the cleaner answer for the inference pods and I'm happy to go that way; the PodSelector / third-party path then only matters for the admin-access DaemonSet case you're already covering in v26.7.0.

@karthikvetrivel Wasn't this already fixed in https://github.com/NVIDIA/gpu-driver-container/commit/446061a33d817484a7be6e3fc78f0671c84e9f72? 

This is essentially `#1` from @yuanchen8911's suggestions:

> 1. The peermem sidecar should treat "module already loaded" as success (check /sys/module or lsmod before the disk modprobe), and/or
> 2. The userspace-only install path should still lay down the kernel-module tree so disk-based modprobe stays valid, and
> 3. k8s-driver-manager should fail hard (retry/backoff) when module unload fails, instead of proceeding into a state the sidecars can't handle.

Although, we should consider implementing `#2` too as it is a more complete solution that addresses the root cause i.e. kernel module tree being wiped out on pod restarts and fast-path not populating it in the new pod.

If there's a genuine module unload, the peermem sidecar should be able to reload since it already runs `chroot /run/nvidia/driver modprobe nvidia-peermem`, and for that reload to work the fast-path also needs lay down the kernel module tree on disk in `/lib/modules/<kernel>`. I'm able to reproduce this on a B200 with host-installed DOCA driver as I test Ubuntu 26.04 driver container. When I `rmmod nvidia_peermem` manually, the sidecar starts crashing because fast path cannot reload `nvidia-peermem` and never recovers until I force a full reinstall (by `rm /run/nvidia/nvidia-driver.state` on the host and restarting driver pod).

I believe `#3` is already true in k8s-driver-manager: https://github.com/NVIDIA/k8s-driver-manager/blob/8b5e354730d295d30f7884c7cec5050fd2b19f2f/cmd/driver-manager/main.go#L768-L785. But it would be good to ensure we only exercise fast-path when modules are deliberately loaded, and not when modules are loaded by accident because cleanup failed.

If your node is stuck in `NotReady` during a container-toolkit deploy, there is a high likelihood that the `containerd` service wasn't restarted successfully. I recommend checking the `journalctl -u containerd` command output for any errors in containerd.

I also see that you mention `containerd v2.3.2`, so you MIGHT be running into `containerd config version mismatch` error. If this is the case, this is explained by some of the inherent limitations in how containerd manages its config. This is a known [issue](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/issues/11747) in `containerd`. To workaround this you have two options:

1. Set the toolkit env var `RUNTIME_CONFIG_SOURCE` .
```
spec:
  toolkit:
    enabled: true
    version: v1.18.1
    env:
    - name: RUNTIME_CONFIG_SOURCE
      value: "file=</path/to/containerd/config/file>"
```
2. Enable [NRI Plugin mode](https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/cloud-native/gpu-operator/latest/cdi.html#container-device-interface-cdi-and-node-resource-interface-nri-plugin-support). Worth keeping in mind that this feature is in Technical Preview (as of the time of posting this comment)

nvidia-dcgm-exporter-dra-cjm8h   0/1     Terminating   3          2m

nvidia-dra-validator-tcxvg       0/1     Terminating   4          2m
nvidia-dra-validator-xxg2k       0/1     Terminating   4          2m
root@ipp1-3494:~# kgpo
NAME                             READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
nvidia-dcgm-exporter-dra-cjm8h   0/1     Terminating   3          2m14s
nvidia-dcgm-exporter-dra-sgknc   0/1     Terminating   4          2m14s
nvidia-dra-validator-tcxvg       0/1     Terminating   4          2m14s
nvidia-dra-validator-xxg2k       0/1     Terminating   4          2m14s
root@ipp1-3494:~#

Both nvidia-dcgm-exporter-dra and nvidia-dra-validator Pods use DRA ResourceClaimTemplates with adminAccess. When Helm deletes the GPUCluster, the PR’s generic ownership model garbage-collects every GPUCluster-owned object, including the DRA kubelet-plugin DaemonSet, concurrently with those workload Pods. The kubelet then cannot call the plugin to unprepare the claims, leaving the Pods stuck in Terminating.

Thanks for the feature request and the detailed use case.

Securely using a signed private APT repository is already possible with the existing `repoConfig` support: include both the repository `.list` file and the public `.asc` key in the ConfigMap, then reference the key explicitly with `signed-by`, for example:

```text
deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/sources.list.d/private-repo.asc] http://ubuntu.mirror ubuntu main
```

APT does not parse the `.asc` file as a repository definition, but it may emit a notice that the file is ignored while scanning `/etc/apt/sources.list.d`, since only `.list` and `.sources` are valid source-list filename extensions. The key can nevertheless be used successfully through the explicit `signed-by` reference.

A dedicated GPG-key configuration would provide a cleaner conventional keyring location and avoid this notice, but it is a usability enhancement rather than a requirement for securely using private repositories. We have not received other customer requests for this capability, so we do not currently plan to prioritize it.

Could you share a concrete example of any issue beyond the APT notice with the existing `repoConfig` approach? That would help us understand whether there is a case the current configuration cannot support.

Confirmed — this fixed it for me on AKS Ubuntu 24.04 / containerd 2.3.2 / GPU Operator v25.10.1. The root cause is that the toolkit's default CLI-based config retrieval (`containerd config dump`) doesn't play nicely with containerd 2.3.x on AKS, triggering the reload/signal issue described above. Forcing file-based config retrieval avoids it entirely — no need for CDI changes, NRI, or `defaultRuntime` changes.

Affected nodes continuously report: 
ContainerRuntimeProblem=True 
ContainerRuntimeIsDown: containerd service is not running, exit code: 3 
KubeletProblem=True 
KubeletIsDown: kubelet service is not running, exit code: 3  

**Fix:** add `RUNTIME_CONFIG_SOURCE=file` to the toolkit env in your `ClusterPolicy`:

```yaml
spec:
  toolkit:
    enabled: true
    version: v1.18.1
    env:
    - name: RUNTIME_CONFIG_SOURCE
      value: file
```

**To apply without a full uninstall/reinstall:**

If you're managing via Helm:
```bash
helm upgrade gpu-operator nvidia/gpu-operator \
  -n gpu-operator \
  -f values.yaml   # values.yaml containing the toolkit.env block above
```

Or patch the existing `ClusterPolicy` CR directly:
```bash
kubectl patch clusterpolicy cluster-policy --type merge -p '
spec:
  toolkit:
    env:
    - name: RUNTIME_CONFIG_SOURCE
      value: file
'
```
(⚠️ this replaces the full `toolkit.env` array, so include any other env vars you already have set, e.g. `CONTAINERD_SOCKET`/`CONTAINERD_CONFIG`, in the same patch)

After applying, the `nvidia-container-toolkit-daemonset` pods restart and stay `Running` past the ~18 min mark that previously triggered the crash:
```bash
kubectl rollout status daemonset -n gpu-operator nvidia-container-toolkit-daemonset
kubectl get pods -n gpu-operator -w
```

Might be worth calling out `RUNTIME_CONFIG_SOURCE=file` as a recommended default (or at least a documented workaround) for AKS Ubuntu 24.04 + containerd 2.x combos until the NRI Plugin path officially supports containerd 2.3.x.

On reflection, the point about "won't be blocked indefinitely because it has no resource requests" doesn't seem entirely true. 

Kubernetes' NodeResourcesFit plugin checks a node's pod-count ceiling (status.allocatable.pods, kubelet's --max-pods, default 110) for every pod unconditionally — this happens before any CPU/memory check, so it applies regardless of what the pod itself requests:

 // pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/noderesources/fit.go
 allowedPodNumber := nodeInfo.GetAllocatable().GetAllowedPodNumber()
 if len(nodeInfo.GetPods())+1 > allowedPodNumber {
     insufficientResources = append(insufficientResources, InsufficientResource{
         ResourceName: v1.ResourcePods,
         Reason:       "Too many pods",

So a zero-request pod like nvidia-vgpu-device-manager is exposed to the same equal-priority preemption gap once a node's pod-count fills up — no CPU/memory pressure needed, just pod density. 

Doesn't change the reconciliation-methodology point (that one's on me), but the conclusion of "no functional impact"  may not do justice to the full picture :)

Any thoughts?

Actually, yes — the production incident behind [#140984](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/140984) was precisely this mechanism: both stuck nodes were at capacity.pods=110 / allocatable.pods=110, exactly at the ceiling, and the scheduler event was Too many pods — not a CPU/memory failure. 
So there's direct production evidence of pod-density-triggered stalls with this exact signature, just on a plain DaemonSet rather than vgpu-device-manager specifically. 
Just putting the facts on the table — happy to leave the call on whether that's enough to act on with you. :)


 Edited to add: one qualifier worth spelling out — once elevated to system-node-critical, this would only actually strand the pod if a large share of the node's pod budget were also at that same tier, which isn't the norm on typical clusters (most of a node's pods are regular workloads at lower priority, and default max-pods is 110). So the mechanism is real, but hitting it specifically for this already-elevated DaemonSet is possible, likely rare in practice — meaningfully rarer than the #140984 production case, where the blocking pods shared the same, unelevated priority as the stuck DaemonSet.

Talos uses [system extensions](https://docs.siderolabs.com/talos/v1.13/build-and-extend-talos/custom-images-and-development/system-extensions) (container images) that are used for adding drivers to the base OS. This is similar to [systemd System Extensions](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd-sysext.html) (raw volumes) because the file system is read only and kernel modules are signed with ephemeral signing keys for each build of Talos.

Our guidance disables the driver integration and toolkit because both of those are provided as part of the base OS configuration.

The way that Talos images are built cryptographically requires that modules and extensions are built (or at least signed) by the same key, ideally in the same CI job that the kernel for Talos image is created.

Hi @anoopsinghnegi , `upgrade-failed` is a failure state, but it is intentionally recoverable. As you have seen, labeling node back to `upgrade-required` lets the upgrade-controller retry the upgrade. If upgrade-controller finds that the node is already upgraded, then it skips the steps which are not required to be done again and transitions the node to `upgrade-done` state. We don't unnecessarily evict workloads and do driver upgrades if nothing is going to be done (system is already in upgraded state). It only retries the steps which needs an action. Since in your case, the upgrade failed at the very end and then by the time it was labeled back to `upgrade-required` after fixing the issue, there was nothing else required and hence the upgrade controller moved the node to `upgrade-done` state.

I am going to close this issue as this is expected. Also you were transitioning from precompiled to compiled in your steps which doesn't go through upgrade controller and have already been explained in prior comment. Please feel free to comment or re-open if you still have any concerns with the workflow.

I'd like to explain my case.


A concrete Ubuntu example is kernel `6.8.0-94-generic` (package version `6.8.0-94.96`). It was included in the Ubuntu 24.04 Noble cloud image release `release-20260131`, after being published to `noble-updates` on 29 January 2026.
This kernel was later removed from the regular Noble package indexes between 15 and 16 June 2026. Therefore, a node created from that cloud image can still be running `6.8.0-94-generic`, while `linux-headers-6.8.0-94-generic` is no longer resolvable from the current Ubuntu repositories.
This is exactly the use case for the separate **`inet` profile**: it uses an immutable Ubuntu Snapshot Service URL, such as the 5 February 2026 snapshot, where the matching headers are still available. It is not the local/private-repository approach.
The **local/private-repository approach** is a separate configuration for restricted environments. It points APT to internal mirrors and supplies their signing keys. Here, `repoConfig` is additive: it mounts ConfigMap entries into `/etc/apt/sources.list.d/` but does not replace source files already present in the NVIDIA driver image. To use only local repositories, the ConfigMap must include empty overrides using the same filenames as the image’s upstream Ubuntu and CUDA source files; otherwise APT continues to use both local and upstream repositories.
In both cases, the existing `repoConfig` mechanism works. For local mirrors, however, a native `gpgKeyConfig` field would still be cleaner than mounting key files alongside repository definitions.

#! /bin/bash

set -eu

RUN_DIR=/run/nvidia

    nscq_package_name=libnvidia-nscq
  else
    nscq_package_name=libnvidia-nscq-${DRIVER_BRANCH}
  fi
  apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ${nscq_package_name}=${DRIVER_VERSION}*
  apt-mark hold ${nscq_package_name}
}

imex_install() {
  local imex_package_name
  if [ "$DRIVER_BRANCH" -ge "580" ]; then
    imex_package_name=nvidia-imex
  elif [ "$DRIVER_BRANCH" -ge "550" ]; then
    imex_package_name=nvidia-imex-${DRIVER_BRANCH}
  else
    return 0
  fi
  apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ${imex_package_name}=${DRIVER_VERSION}*
  apt-mark hold ${imex_package_name}
}

nvlink5_pkgs_install() {
  if [ "$DRIVER_BRANCH" -ge "570" ]; then
    apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends nvlsm
    apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends infiniband-diags
  fi
}

# libnvsdm packages are not available for arm64
nvsdm_install() {
  local nvsdm_package_name
  if [ "$TARGETARCH" = "amd64" ]; then
    if [ "$DRIVER_BRANCH" -ge "580" ]; then
      nvsdm_package_name=libnvsdm
    elif [ "$DRIVER_BRANCH" -ge "560" ]; then

    fi
    apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ${nvsdm_package_name}=${DRIVER_VERSION}*
    apt-mark hold ${nvsdm_package_name}
  fi
}

_update_package_cache() {
    if [ "${PACKAGE_TAG:-}" != "builtin" ]; then
        echo "Updating the package cache..."
        if ! apt-get -qq update; then
            echo "ERROR: Failed to update package cache. "\
                 "Ensure that the cluster can access the proper networks."
            exit 1
        fi
    fi
}

_assert_nvswitch_system() {
    [ -d /proc/driver/nvidia-nvswitch/devices ] || return 1
    if [ -z "$(ls -A /proc/driver/nvidia-nvswitch/devices)" ]; then
        return 1
    fi
    return 0
}

_assert_nvlink5_system() (
    for dir in /sys/class/infiniband/*/device; do
        # Define the path to the VPD file
        vpd_file="$dir/vpd"

        # Check if the VPD file exists
        if [ -f "$vpd_file" ]; then
            # Search for 'SW_MNG' in the VPD file
            if grep -q "SW_MNG" "$vpd_file"; then
                echo "Detected NVLink5+ system"
                return 0
            fi
        fi
    done
    return 1
)

_ensure_nvlink5_prerequisites() (
    until  lsmod | grep mlx5_core > /dev/null 2>&1 && lsmod | grep ib_umad > /dev/null 2>&1;
    do
        echo "waiting for the mlx5_core and ib_umad kernel modules to be loaded"
        sleep 10
    done
)

# Check if mellanox devices are present
_mellanox_devices_present() {
    devices_found=0
    for dev in /sys/bus/pci/devices/*; do
        read vendor < $dev/vendor
        if [ "$vendor" = "0x15b3" ]; then
            echo "Mellanox device found at $(basename $dev)"
            return 0
        fi
    done
    echo "No Mellanox devices were found..."
    return 1
}

_gpu_direct_rdma_enabled() {
    if [ "${GPU_DIRECT_RDMA_ENABLED}" = "true" ]; then
        # check if mellanox cards are present
        if  _mellanox_devices_present; then
            return 0
        fi
    fi
    return 1
}

# For each kernel module configuration file mounted into the container,
# parse the file contents and extract the custom module parameters that
# are to be passed as input to 'modprobe'.
#
# Assumptions:
# - Configuration files are named <module-name>.conf (i.e. nvidia.conf, nvidia-uvm.conf).
# - Configuration files are mounted inside the container at /drivers.
# - Each line in the file contains at least one parameter, where parameters on the same line
#   are space delimited. It is up to the user to properly format the file to ensure
#   the correct set of parameters are passed to 'modprobe'.
_get_module_params() {
    local base_path="/drivers"
    # nvidia
    if [ -f "${base_path}/nvidia.conf" ]; then
       while IFS="" read -r param || [ -n "$param" ]; do
           NVIDIA_MODULE_PARAMS+=("$param")
       done <"${base_path}/nvidia.conf"
       echo "Module parameters provided for nvidia: ${NVIDIA_MODULE_PARAMS[@]}"
    fi
    # nvidia-uvm
    if [ -f "${base_path}/nvidia-uvm.conf" ]; then
       while IFS="" read -r param || [ -n "$param" ]; do
           NVIDIA_UVM_MODULE_PARAMS+=("$param")
       done <"${base_path}/nvidia-uvm.conf"
       echo "Module parameters provided for nvidia-uvm: ${NVIDIA_UVM_MODULE_PARAMS[@]}"
    fi
    # nvidia-modeset
    if [ -f "${base_path}/nvidia-modeset.conf" ]; then
       while IFS="" read -r param || [ -n "$param" ]; do
           NVIDIA_MODESET_MODULE_PARAMS+=("$param")
       done <"${base_path}/nvidia-modeset.conf"
       echo "Module parameters provided for nvidia-modeset: ${NVIDIA_MODESET_MODULE_PARAMS[@]}"
    fi
    # nvidia-peermem
    if [ -f "${base_path}/nvidia-peermem.conf" ]; then
       while IFS="" read -r param || [ -n "$param" ]; do
           NVIDIA_PEERMEM_MODULE_PARAMS+=("$param")
       done <"${base_path}/nvidia-peermem.conf"
       echo "Module parameters provided for nvidia-peermem: ${NVIDIA_PEERMEM_MODULE_PARAMS[@]}"
    fi
}

_create_module_params_conf() {
    echo "Parsing kernel module parameters..."
    _get_module_params

    if [ ${#NVIDIA_MODULE_PARAMS[@]} -gt 0 ]; then
        echo "Configuring nvidia module parameters in ${MODPROBE_CONFIG_DIR}/nvidia.conf"
        echo "options nvidia ${NVIDIA_MODULE_PARAMS[@]}" > ${MODPROBE_CONFIG_DIR}/nvidia.conf
    fi
    if [ ${#NVIDIA_UVM_MODULE_PARAMS[@]} -gt 0 ]; then
        echo "Configuring nvidia-uvm module parameters in ${MODPROBE_CONFIG_DIR}/nvidia-uvm.conf"
        echo "options nvidia-uvm ${NVIDIA_UVM_MODULE_PARAMS[@]}" > ${MODPROBE_CONFIG_DIR}/nvidia-uvm.conf
    fi
    if [ ${#NVIDIA_MODESET_MODULE_PARAMS[@]} -gt 0 ]; then
        echo "Configuring nvidia-modeset module parameters in ${MODPROBE_CONFIG_DIR}/nvidia-modeset.conf"
        echo "options nvidia-modeset ${NVIDIA_MODESET_MODULE_PARAMS[@]}" > ${MODPROBE_CONFIG_DIR}/nvidia-modeset.conf
    fi
    if [ ${#NVIDIA_PEERMEM_MODULE_PARAMS[@]} -gt 0 ]; then
        echo "Configuring nvidia-peermem module parameters in ${MODPROBE_CONFIG_DIR}/nvidia-peermem.conf"
        echo "options nvidia-peermem ${NVIDIA_PEERMEM_MODULE_PARAMS[@]}" > ${MODPROBE_CONFIG_DIR}/nvidia-peermem.conf
    fi
}

# Load the kernel modules and start persistenced.
_load_driver() {
    local nv_fw_search_path="$RUN_DIR/driver/lib/firmware"
    local set_fw_path="true"
    local fw_path_config_file="/sys/module/firmware_class/parameters/path"
    for param in "${NVIDIA_MODULE_PARAMS[@]}"; do
        if [[ "$param" == "NVreg_EnableGpuFirmware=0" ]]; then
          set_fw_path="false"
        fi
    done

    if [[ "$set_fw_path" == "true" ]]; then
        echo "Configuring the following firmware search path in '$fw_path_config_file': $nv_fw_search_path"
        if [[ ! -z $(grep '[^[:space:]]' $fw_path_config_file) ]]; then
            echo "WARNING: A search path is already configured in $fw_path_config_file"
            echo "         Retaining the current configuration"
        else
            echo -n "$nv_fw_search_path" > $fw_path_config_file || echo "WARNING: Failed to configure firmware search path"
        fi
    fi

    echo "Loading ipmi and i2c_core kernel modules..."
    modprobe -a i2c_core ipmi_msghandler ipmi_devintf

    echo "Loading NVIDIA driver kernel modules..."
    set -o xtrace +o nounset
    modprobe nvidia
    modprobe nvidia-uvm
    modprobe nvidia-modeset
    set +o xtrace -o nounset


    if _gpu_direct_rdma_enabled; then
        echo "Loading NVIDIA Peer Memory kernel module..."
        set -o xtrace +o nounset
        modprobe nvidia-peermem
        set +o xtrace -o nounset
    fi

    echo "Starting NVIDIA persistence daemon..."
    nvidia-persistenced --persistence-mode

    DRIVER_VERSION=$(nvidia-smi -q | grep "Driver Version" | awk -F: '{print $2}' | xargs)
    if _assert_nvlink5_system; then
        _ensure_nvlink5_prerequisites || return 1

        echo "Installing NVIDIA fabric manager, libnvsdm and nvlsm packages..."
        nvlink5_pkgs_install
        fabricmanager_install
        nvsdm_install
        imex_install

        echo "Starting NVIDIA fabric manager daemon for NVLink5+..."

        fm_config_file=/usr/share/nvidia/nvswitch/fabricmanager.cfg
        fm_pid_file=/var/run/nvidia-fabricmanager/nv-fabricmanager.pid
        nvlsm_config_file=/usr/share/nvidia/nvlsm/nvlsm.conf
        nvlsm_pid_file=/var/run/nvidia-fabricmanager/nvlsm.pid
        /usr/bin/nvidia-fabricmanager-start.sh --mode start \
                                               --fm-config-file $fm_config_file \
                                               --fm-pid-file $fm_pid_file \
                                               --nvlsm-config-file $nvlsm_config_file \
                                               --nvlsm-pid-file $nvlsm_pid_file

    # If not a NVLink5+ switch, check for the presence of NVLink4 (or below) switches
    elif _assert_nvswitch_system; then
        echo "Installing NVIDIA fabric manager and libnvidia NSCQ packages..."
        fabricmanager_install
        nscq_install
        imex_install
 
        echo "Starting NVIDIA fabric manager daemon..."
        nv-fabricmanager -c /usr/share/nvidia/nvswitch/fabricmanager.cfg
    fi

    return 0
}

# Stop persistenced and unload the kernel modules if they are currently loaded.
_unload_driver() {
    local rmmod_args=()
    local nvidia_deps=0
    local nvidia_refs=0
    local nvidia_uvm_refs=0
    local nvidia_modeset_refs=0
    local nvidia_peermem_refs=0

    if [ -f /var/run/nvidia-persistenced/nvidia-persistenced.pid ]; then
        echo "Stopping NVIDIA persistence daemon..."
        local pid=$(< /var/run/nvidia-persistenced/nvidia-persistenced.pid)

        kill -SIGTERM "${pid}"
        for i in $(seq 1 50); do
            kill -0 "${pid}" 2> /dev/null || break
            sleep 0.1
        done
        if [ $i -eq 50 ]; then
            echo "Could not stop NVIDIA persistence daemon" >&2
            return 1
        fi
    fi

    if [ -f /var/run/nvidia-fabricmanager/nv-fabricmanager.pid ]; then
        echo "Stopping NVIDIA fabric manager daemon..."
        local pid=$(< /var/run/nvidia-fabricmanager/nv-fabricmanager.pid)

        kill -SIGTERM "${pid}"
        for i in $(seq 1 50); do
            kill -0 "${pid}" 2> /dev/null || break
            sleep 0.1
        done
        if [ $i -eq 50 ]; then
            echo "Could not stop NVIDIA fabric manager daemon" >&2
            return 1
        fi
    fi

    if [ -f /var/run/nvidia-fabricmanager/nvlsm.pid ]; then
        echo "Stopping NVLink Subnet Manager daemon..."
        local pid=$(< /var/run/nvidia-fabricmanager/nvlsm.pid)

        kill -SIGTERM "${pid}"
        for i in $(seq 1 50); do
            kill -0 "${pid}" 2> /dev/null || break
            sleep 0.1
        done
        if [ $i -eq 50 ]; then
            echo "Could not stop NVLink Subnet Manager daemon" >&2
            return 1
        fi
    fi

    echo "Unloading NVIDIA driver kernel modules..."
    if [ -f /sys/module/nvidia_drm/refcnt ]; then
        nvidia_drm_refs=$(< /sys/module/nvidia_drm/refcnt)
        rmmod_args+=("nvidia-drm")
        ((++nvidia_deps))
    fi
    if [ -f /sys/module/nvidia_modeset/refcnt ]; then
        nvidia_modeset_refs=$(< /sys/module/nvidia_modeset/refcnt)
        rmmod_args+=("nvidia-modeset")
        ((++nvidia_deps))
    fi
    if [ -f /sys/module/nvidia_uvm/refcnt ]; then
        nvidia_uvm_refs=$(< /sys/module/nvidia_uvm/refcnt)
        rmmod_args+=("nvidia-uvm")
        ((++nvidia_deps))
    fi
    if [ -f /sys/module/nvidia_peermem/refcnt ]; then
        nvidia_peermem_refs=$(< /sys/module/nvidia_peermem/refcnt)
        rmmod_args+=("nvidia-peermem")
        ((++nvidia_deps))
    fi
    if [ -f /sys/module/nvidia/refcnt ]; then
        nvidia_refs=$(< /sys/module/nvidia/refcnt)
        rmmod_args+=("nvidia")
    fi
    if [ ${nvidia_refs} -gt ${nvidia_deps} ]; then
        # run lsmod to debug module usage
        lsmod | grep nvidia
        echo "Could not unload NVIDIA driver kernel modules, driver is in use" >&2
        return 1
    fi

    if [ ${#rmmod_args[@]} -gt 0 ]; then
        rmmod ${rmmod_args[@]}
    fi
    return 0
}

_resolve_kernel_type_from_driver_branch() {
  [[ "${DRIVER_BRANCH}" -lt 560 ]] && KERNEL_TYPE=kernel || KERNEL_TYPE=kernel-open
}

# _resolve_kernel_type determines which kernel module type, open or proprietary, to install.
# This function assumes that the nvidia-installer binary is in the PATH, so this function
# should only be invoked after the userspace driver components have been installed.
#
# KERNEL_MODULE_TYPE is the frontend interface that users can use to configure which module
# to install. Valid values for KERNEL_MODULE_TYPE are 'auto' (default), 'open', and 'proprietary'.
# When 'auto' is configured, we use the nvidia-installer to recommend the module type to install.
_resolve_kernel_type() {
  if [ "${KERNEL_MODULE_TYPE}" == "proprietary" ]; then
    KERNEL_TYPE=kernel
  elif [ "${KERNEL_MODULE_TYPE}" == "open" ]; then
    KERNEL_TYPE=kernel-open
  elif [ "${KERNEL_MODULE_TYPE}" == "auto" ]; then
    kernel_module_type=$(nvidia-installer --print-recommended-kernel-module-type 2> /dev/null)
    if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
      echo "failed to retrieve the recommended kernel module type from nvidia-installer, falling back to using the driver branch"
      _resolve_kernel_type_from_driver_branch
      return 0
    fi
    [[ "${kernel_module_type}" == "open" ]] && KERNEL_TYPE=kernel-open || KERNEL_TYPE=kernel
  else
    echo "invalid value for the KERNEL_MODULE_TYPE variable: ${KERNEL_MODULE_TYPE}"
    return 1
  fi
}

# Link and install the kernel modules from a precompiled packages
_install_driver() {
    apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
        nvidia-utils-${DRIVER_BRANCH}-server \
        nvidia-headless-no-dkms-${DRIVER_BRANCH}-server \
        libnvidia-decode-${DRIVER_BRANCH}-server \
        libnvidia-extra-${DRIVER_BRANCH}-server \
        libnvidia-encode-${DRIVER_BRANCH}-server \
        libnvidia-fbc1-${DRIVER_BRANCH}-server \
        libnvidia-gl-${DRIVER_BRANCH}-server

    # Now install the precompiled kernel module packages signed by Canonical
    if [ "$KERNEL_TYPE" = "kernel-open" ]; then
        echo "Installing Open NVIDIA driver kernel modules..."
        apt-get install --no-install-recommends -y \
            linux-signatures-nvidia-${KERNEL_VERSION} \
            linux-modules-nvidia-${DRIVER_BRANCH}-server-open-${KERNEL_VERSION}
    else
        echo "Installing Closed NVIDIA driver kernel modules..."
        apt-get install --no-install-recommends -y \
            linux-objects-nvidia-${DRIVER_BRANCH}-server-${KERNEL_VERSION} \
            linux-signatures-nvidia-${KERNEL_VERSION} \
            linux-modules-nvidia-${DRIVER_BRANCH}-server-${KERNEL_VERSION}
    fi
}

# Mount the driver rootfs into the run directory with the exception of sysfs.
_mount_rootfs() {
    echo "Mounting NVIDIA driver rootfs..."

    mount --make-runbindable /sys
    mount --make-private /sys

    mkdir -p ${RUN_DIR}/driver

    # Export the full container rootfs
    mount --rbind / ${RUN_DIR}/driver

    # Ensure proper propagation to host
    mount --make-rslave ${RUN_DIR}/driver

    # Optional but safe: ensure /dev propagation (fixes some CRI issues)
    if [ ! -d "${RUN_DIR}/driver/dev" ]; then
        mkdir -p ${RUN_DIR}/driver/dev
    fi
   
    mount --rbind /dev ${RUN_DIR}/driver/dev
    mount --make-rslave ${RUN_DIR}/driver/dev
}

# Unmount the driver rootfs from the run directory.
_unmount_rootfs() {
    echo "Unmounting NVIDIA driver rootfs..."
    if findmnt -r -o TARGET | grep "${RUN_DIR}/driver" > /dev/null; then
        umount -l -R ${RUN_DIR}/driver
    fi
}

init() {
    # Determine the kernel module type
    _resolve_kernel_type || exit 1

    echo -e "\n========== NVIDIA Software Installer ==========\n"
    echo -e "Starting installation of NVIDIA driver branch ${DRIVER_BRANCH} for Linux kernel version ${KERNEL_VERSION}\n"

    exec 3> ${PID_FILE}
    if ! flock -n 3; then
        echo "An instance of the NVIDIA driver is already running, aborting"
        exit 1
    fi
    echo $$ >&3

    trap "echo 'Caught signal'; exit 1" HUP INT QUIT PIPE TERM
    trap "_shutdown" EXIT

    _unload_driver || exit 1
    _unmount_rootfs

    _update_package_cache

    _create_module_params_conf
    _install_driver
    _load_driver || exit 1
    _mount_rootfs

    echo "Create symlink for the vulkan icd"
    ln -s  /run/nvidia/driver/usr/share/vulkan/icd.d/nvidia_icd.json  /run/nvidia/driver/etc/vulkan/icd.d/nvidia_icd.json

    echo "Done, now waiting for signal"
    sleep infinity &
    trap "echo 'Caught signal'; _shutdown && { kill $!; exit 0; }" HUP INT QUIT PIPE TERM
    trap - EXIT
    while true; do wait $! || continue; done
    exit 0
}

_shutdown() {
    if _unload_driver; then
        _unmount_rootfs
        rm -f ${PID_FILE}
        return 0
    fi
    return 1
}

# Wait for MOFED drivers to be loaded and load nvidia-peermem whenever it gets unloaded during MOFED driver updates
reload_nvidia_peermem() {
    if [ "$USE_HOST_MOFED" = "true" ]; then
        until  lsmod | grep mlx5_core > /dev/null 2>&1 && [ -f /sys/module/nvidia/refcnt ];
        do
            echo "waiting for mellanox ofed and nvidia drivers to be installed"
            sleep 10
        done
    else
        # use driver readiness flag created by MOFED container
        until  [ -f /run/mellanox/drivers/.driver-ready ] && [ -f /sys/module/nvidia/refcnt ];
        do
            echo "waiting for mellanox ofed and nvidia drivers to be installed"
            sleep 10
        done
    fi
    # get any parameters provided for nvidia-peermem
    _get_module_params && set +o nounset
    if chroot /run/nvidia/driver modprobe nvidia-peermem "${NVIDIA_PEERMEM_MODULE_PARAMS[@]}"; then
        if [ -f /sys/module/nvidia_peermem/refcnt ]; then
            echo "successfully loaded nvidia-peermem module, now waiting for signal"
            sleep inf
            trap "echo 'Caught signal'; exit 1" HUP INT QUIT PIPE TERM
        fi
    fi
    echo "failed to load nvidia-peermem module"
    exit 1
}

# probe by gpu-opertor for liveness/startup checks for nvidia-peermem module to be loaded when MOFED drivers are ready
probe_nvidia_peermem() {
    if lsmod | grep mlx5_core > /dev/null 2>&1; then
        if [ ! -f /sys/module/nvidia_peermem/refcnt ]; then
            echo "nvidia-peermem module is not loaded"
            return 1
        fi
    else
        echo "MOFED drivers are not ready, skipping probe to avoid container restarts..."
    fi
    return 0
}

usage() {
    cat >&2 <<EOF
Usage: $0 COMMAND [ARG...]

Commands:
  init   [-a | --accept-license]
  update [-k | --kernel VERSION] [-s | --sign KEYID] [-t | --tag TAG]
EOF
    exit 1
}

if [ $# -eq 0 ]; then
    usage
fi
command=$1; shift
case "${command}" in
    init) options=$(getopt -l accept-license -o a -- "$@") ;;
    reload_nvidia_peermem) options="" ;;
    probe_nvidia_peermem) options="" ;;
    *) usage ;;
esac
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
    usage
fi

$command
```

Thanks, this is very helpful. We reviewed the pod timeline and the custom driver-image changes.

The pod status shows that the current driver cycle is not validated:
`nvidia-cuda-validator` completed at age 73m.
The current `nvidia-driver-daemonset` pod was created later, at age 64m.
The current `nvidia-operator-validator` pod was created at age 62m and remains in Init:0/4.
Therefore, the completed CUDA validator belongs to the previous driver cycle. The current validator is correctly blocked in driver-validation; this snapshot is not a validator Ready false-positive.
The driver pod being `1/1 Ready` means its startup probe succeeded. That probe executes `nvidia-driver-startup-probe` and writes `/run/nvidia/validations/.driver-ctr-ready`. Since `/run/nvidia/validations` is empty on the host, the marker was either removed after it was written or the host and driver container are observing different mounts.

We also noticed that the custom image changes `_mount_rootfs()` from the upstream GPU Driver Container implementation. Specifically, it adds:
```
mount --make-rslave ${RUN_DIR}/driver
mount --rbind /dev ${RUN_DIR}/driver/dev
mount --make-rslave ${RUN_DIR}/driver/dev
```

`rslave` is not bidirectional propagation; mount events below it do not propagate back to the host. These changes can affect visibility of /run/nvidia/driver/dev device nodes in the legacy, non-CDI path. The upstream driver container already supports that legacy rootfs-mount approach, so please reproduce with these custom mount changes removed while retaining the secure-boot driver packaging.

Two things I found against my own #2603. Both change what it is worth.

The reboot rationale in that PR is wrong. MIG mode persistence and the reset requirement are inverted across generations: on Ampere the mode survives a reboot through the InfoROM status bit but enabling it needs a GPU reset, and from Hopper the bit is gone, so the mode is lost on driver reload but enabling needs no reset. Those two sets do not overlap, so restoring MIG mode after a reboot never needs a reset on any generation. I have rewritten the PR body to the narrower case that does hold: on Ampere the driver's own reset attempt can fail, refused while the GPU is in use or disallowed by the hypervisor under passthrough, leaving `mig.mode.pending=Enabled` with `mig.mode.current` not `Enabled`.

The second one is less settled. The guard skips any GPU with `numVFs > 0`, reasoning that VFs do not survive a reboot so a GPU that has them has a VM attached. That reasoning is false. VFs come from `sriov-manage -e ALL` at driver load, which is how `isDriverUsingSRIOV` reads `NumVFs > 0` in the same file. VFs being up is the normal state with no VMs anywhere. Whether that makes the feature a no-op depends on whether VFs are already up at the moment validation runs, and that is startup ordering I have not observed on hardware.

Together: the stated trigger does not need the feature, and the guard may stop it firing in the case that does. Worth settling before anyone spends review time on the design.

The VF guard in `commitMIGMode` looks wrong in both directions, so I think it needs rework rather than a comment explaining it.

The same file treats VF state as volatile in one function and constant in another. `waitForParentDevices` calls `nvpci.New().GetGPUs()` inside its poll loop and returns `AreAllVFsReady(gpus)`, re-reading every tick because the state changes underneath it. `commitMIGMode`, which runs just before it, reads that state once at the top and holds it across two `chroot`/`nvidia-smi` calls, `queryMIGModes` and `gpuHasRunningProcesses`, before `--gpu-reset` runs. The `numVFs > 0` check still uses the first read, so a card that gets VFs in between can be reset anyway.

`gpuHasRunningProcesses` goes the other way. It returns `strings.TrimSpace(string(out)) != ""`, so any non-empty output from `--query-compute-apps=pid` is treated as running work. If that query returns anything that is not a PID list, the guard never passes and no reset happens.

Also the guard under test is not the one that runs. `shouldResetForMIGCommit` is called after two `continue`s have already made `needsCommit()` true and `numVFs` zero, so it reduces to `!busy` there. The real check is the inline `if numVFs > 0`, and nothing covers it. The "VFs still enabled" table cases pass without touching the production path.

`newTestPF(totalVFs, numVFs)` is already in the test file, and `isDriverUsingSRIOV`/`AreAllVFsReady` are free functions. Pulling the selection up to the VF gate into something like `gpusNeedingMIGCommit(gpus, modes)` would not need an exec seam, since the VF check short-circuits before the busy probe. It would cover the address join too.

Walkthrough

The validator now initializes Kubernetes clients in `start` and passes them to selected components. Component validation, workload-config reads, and driver-management checks use the supplied clients instead of creating clients locally. `NodeMetrics` stores a Kubernetes client and reuses it in device-plugin and driver validation watchers.
Merge Risk: Low · up to 6aecd

The refactor removes duplicate client setup, but it moves client creation ahead of checks that did not need the API. If in-cluster client setup fails, validation that used to succeed now errors. With status-file cleanup disabled, stale readiness markers can also remain. Both are narrow and low-likelihood, and the fixes are small.
Security architecture risk: Moderate · up to 6aecd

A validator restart can leave an old success marker in place if Kubernetes client setup fails. Other components can then treat the node as ready even though the current validation did not run. The same startup failure now prevents the metrics exporter from serving local health signals. The review did not establish any expansion of Kubernetes permissions or network access. **Retained concerns** - **Medium · reliability · observed:** Driver, plugin, CUDA, and CC Manager used to remove prior readiness markers before any client setup they needed. Head can return before that removal. With bulk cleanup disabled and a prior marker present, a failed invocation leaves old success visible; on the same node, toolkit and device-plugin startup can accept and source the old driver-ready metadata. - **Low · reliability · observed:** In the base, failure to construct a Kubernetes client in the device-plugin watcher did not prevent the exporter from serving local readiness and PCI metrics. Head requires successful client construction before starting the exporter at all, removing those independent signals during the startup failures they could help diagnose.
Security review details

**Security Blast Radius** - _inferred_ — The demonstrated failure scope is each affected node's validator markers, their consumers, and the node metrics exporter. A common configuration failure could affect multiple nodes independently; the code does not make the client shared across pods or nodes. **Trust Boundaries and Controls** - _observed_ — Startup uses the same in-cluster configuration mechanism as the previous callers. The exporter passes that client to background validation watchers; HTTP scrapes use the Prometheus handler and do not dispatch validation calls. **Hardening Proposals** - _proposed_ — Preserve per-component marker invalidation before fallible client setup, and keep local metrics available while reporting API-dependent checks as unavailable. A process-local client initialized on first use is one way to retain reuse without making unrelated work depend on construction.
